Long 33
Question
Differentiate between controlled and uncontrolled components with examples. …
LongUnit 22.3 Forms — adding, handling & submitting
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: A controlled component is a form control whose current value is supplied by React state through value or checked, with an event handler updating that state. React is the source of truth. An uncontrolled component stores its current editable value in the DOM; React may provide an initial defaultValue/defaultChecked, and code reads the value when needed through a ref or FormData.

Definitions

These terms describe how form values are managed, not whether a component is a class or a function. Both techniques work with function components.

Comparison

Aspect Controlled Uncontrolled
Value owner React state DOM control
Main props value / checked defaultValue / defaultChecked
Reading data Current state Ref or FormData on submission
Per-keystroke logic Easy to derive live validation/UI Requires additional event/state logic if needed
Reset Set state to initial values Native form reset or direct supported control APIs
Typical use Synchronized, dynamic form interfaces Simple forms and some integrations
Common pitfall Missing onChange makes an editable field effectively read-only Changing defaultValue is not a normal way to control edits

Example: complete example of both

Place this file in src/App.jsx of a configured React JSX project. Each form has its own result and submits without navigation.

React · JSX
import {useRef, useState} from "react";

function ControlledName() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
  const [saved, setSaved] = useState("");
  function submit(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    setSaved(name.trim() || "No name entered");
  }
  return <form onSubmit={submit}>
    <h2>Controlled</h2>
    <label>Name <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} /></label>
    <p>Live preview: {name}</p>
    <button type="submit">Save</button><p>Saved: {saved}</p>
  </form>;
}
function UncontrolledName() {
  const nameRef = useRef(null);
  const [saved, setSaved] = useState("");
  function submit(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    setSaved(nameRef.current.value.trim() || "No name entered");
  }
  return <form onSubmit={submit}>
    <h2>Uncontrolled</h2>
    <label>Name <input ref={nameRef} defaultValue="" /></label>
    <button type="submit">Save</button><p>Saved: {saved}</p>
  </form>;
}
export default function App() {
  return <main><ControlledName /><UncontrolledName /></main>;
}

Algorithm and observed behavior

For the controlled form, every edit invokes onChange, updates state and changes both the input and the live preview. For the uncontrolled form, typing changes the DOM's input value without scheduling a React update for that draft value. Submission reads the ref and uses state only for the saved result.

Sample: type Asha into both inputs. The controlled live preview immediately shows Asha; the uncontrolled form has no live draft output. After each Save, the corresponding saved paragraph displays Asha. This illustrates that an uncontrolled input can coexist with other React state in the same component.

Limitations / precautions — edge cases and choice

A controlled input should begin with a suitable value, such as "" for text or false for a checkbox, not switch from undefined to a string later. Do not supply both value and defaultValue to control the same input. File inputs are special: browsers restrict programmatic file selection, so selected files are normally read from the control's files property.

Refs are populated after the element is mounted; event handlers can normally access them, but code should account for unmounting in delayed operations. Neither pattern replaces validation on the server. Choose controlled inputs when live synchronization matters and uncontrolled inputs when submit-time reading is sufficient; avoid assuming one approach is universally faster or safer.

Conclusion: Controlled components keep current values in React state; uncontrolled components read values from the DOM when required. Choose intentionally and avoid changing a control's ownership mode after mounting.

2.4 Hooks

Long 34
Question
⭐⭐ Explain React Hooks in detail. …
LongUnit 22.4 Hooks★ × 2
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Hooks are React APIs that let function components use state, synchronization, context, refs and performance-related features. They were introduced in React 16.8. Before hooks, stateful behavior commonly required classes; function components are no longer limited to stateless presentation.

Definition and purpose

Hooks also make it possible to extract reusable behavior into custom hooks, whose names begin with use. A custom hook reuses logic, not one automatic shared state instance: separate calls normally have separate state unless they explicitly connect to shared context or an external store.

Important hooks

Hook Purpose Key precaution
useState Store a state value and schedule updates Do not mutate objects/arrays directly
useReducer Manage transitions through a reducer Reducer must be pure
useEffect Synchronize with external systems after commit Correct dependencies and cleanup
useContext Read the nearest context provider's value Provider changes may update consumers
useRef Retain a mutable value or DOM reference Ref writes do not cause rendering
useMemo Cache a calculation result Optimization, not persistent storage
useCallback Cache a function reference Include reactive dependencies
useId Generate IDs for accessibility relationships Not a data key generator for lists
useLayoutEffect Perform layout-related synchronization before paint Can block painting; use sparingly

Rules and mental model

Call ordinary hooks at the top level of a component or another custom hook, before conditional returns. Do not call them in loops, conditions, nested callbacks, class methods or event handlers. React relies on consistent hook ordering. Event handlers use the setters returned by hooks; they do not create new hooks.

State is a snapshot for each render. Updating it requests another render rather than changing the current local variable immediately. Effects belong to committed rendering, and cleanup prevents leaked timers/listeners. Keep exhaustive dependency checks enabled instead of suppressing them to force a desired timing. Newer React's special use API has distinct rules; the standard state/effect rules above are the syllabus focus.

Example: complete example with a custom hook

This browser-based App.jsx tracks online status and a local counter in a configured React JSX project.

React · JSX
import {useEffect, useState} from "react";

function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(() => navigator.onLine);
  useEffect(() => {
    function sync() { setOnline(navigator.onLine); }
    window.addEventListener("online", sync);
    window.addEventListener("offline", sync);
    sync();
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener("online", sync);
      window.removeEventListener("offline", sync);
    };
  }, []);
  return online;
}
export default function App() {
  const online = useOnlineStatus();
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <main><h1>Hooks example</h1>
    <p>Browser network status: {online ? "online" : "offline"}</p>
    <p aria-live="polite">Count: {count}</p>
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>Add one</button>
  </main>;
}

Limitations / precautions — working, output and edge cases

Algorithm: initialize the browser status → attach two listeners after mount → update status when events occur → remove the exact same listener functions during cleanup. The counter updates separately through a functional setter. Clicking twice shows Count: 2. Switching the browser's network mode can update the displayed status.

navigator.onLine is only the browser's network indicator; it does not guarantee that a particular website/API is reachable. This example assumes client-side browser rendering. A server-rendered application must guard browser globals and account for hydration consistency.

Benefits

Hooks group logic by concern, reduce class/this boilerplate and support reusable behavior. Misused effects, stale closures and unnecessary memoization can create new complexity, so hooks are not magic performance improvements. Correct ordering, immutable state updates, clear dependencies and reliable cleanup are the essential exam points.

Conclusion: Hooks attach stateful behavior to function components and allow focused logic reuse. Stable call order, effect cleanup and explicit dependencies are essential to that model.

Long 35
Question
Define Hooks in React. Also explain how Hooks are used to maintain state in a functional component. …
LongUnit 22.4 Hooks
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Hooks are functions provided by React that let function components use features such as state and effects. useState is the basic state hook. It returns an array containing the state value for the current render and a setter that requests a later render with a new value.

Definition

Syntax: const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue);. The state is retained while the component keeps the same identity in the tree; an ordinary local variable is recreated on each render and does not provide this memory.

How state is maintained

The initializer is used when that hook state is created, not to reset state on every render. A function initializer, such as useState(() => computeInitialValue()), can defer expensive initialization. It should be pure because development checks may invoke it more than once.

Example: complete example

Save as src/App.jsx in a configured React JSX project. It demonstrates both a number state and an object state without direct mutation.

React · JSX
import {useState} from "react";

export default function App() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const [student, setStudent] = useState({name: "Asha", course: "BCA"});
  const doubleCount = count * 2;
  function addTwo() {
    setCount(previous => previous + 1);
    setCount(previous => previous + 1);
  }
  function rename(event) {
    const name = event.target.value;
    setStudent(previous => ({...previous, name}));
  }
  return <main><h1>State in a function component</h1>
    <p>Count: {count}; double: {doubleCount}</p>
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>Add one</button>
    <button type="button" onClick={addTwo}>Add two</button>
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setCount(0)}>Reset</button>
    <label>Name <input value={student.name} onChange={rename} /></label>
    <p>{student.name || "Unnamed"} studies {student.course}.</p>
  </main>;
}

Algorithm and example output

Initialize count and student → render their values → handle clicks or typing → create the next state → let React re-render. Initially the page displays Count: 0; double: 0 and Asha studies BCA. Clicking Add two once produces Count: 2; double: 4. Replacing Asha with Ravi changes the sentence to Ravi studies BCA, while retaining the course.

The double is derived directly from count instead of stored separately, preventing two state values from becoming inconsistent. The object update uses spread because a hook setter replaces its value rather than shallowly merging it like class setState does.

State snapshots and queued updates

Two calls to setCount(count + 1) in the same handler typically both refer to the same captured count and request the same next value. Functional updaters instead receive pending state in sequence, so the two updates in addTwo reliably add two. Do not rely on reading an immediately changed count variable after invoking the setter; it remains the current render's snapshot.

Limitations / precautions — rules, edge cases

Call useState at the top level, not conditionally or inside the click handler. Copy every changed nesting level in object/array state; spread is shallow. If the next value is equal by React's comparison, React may skip an unnecessary update. Component unmounting or an identity/key change resets local memory. Hooks maintain state through React's rendering system, not by turning function-local variables into global storage.

Conclusion: useState preserves a value for a component's identity and supplies a setter that queues later rendering. Functional updates and immutable values avoid common stale-state and mutation errors.

Long 36
Question
What are Hooks in React? Write the rules to be followed while using Hooks. Also explain useState() and useEffect() with example. …
LongUnit 22.4 Hooks
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Hooks allow function components to use state, effects and other React features. For ordinary hooks such as useState and useEffect, the core rules are:

Hooks and their rules

  1. Call hooks only from React function components or custom hooks.
  2. Call them at the top level, before conditional returns—not in loops, conditions, nested functions or event handlers.
  3. Keep the order of calls consistent across renders.
  4. Keep render logic and state updater calculations pure; do not mutate state objects.
  5. Include all reactive values used by an effect in its dependency list, unless the code is restructured so they are no longer dependencies.
  6. Return cleanup for ongoing work such as timers/listeners/subscriptions, and use the hook linter rather than silencing warnings blindly.

An event handler can invoke setCount; it must not call useState to create new state. React's newer special use API has its own exceptions and should not be confused with these standard syllabus hooks.

useState()

const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue) gives persistent component memory. A setter queues the next render. When the next value depends on the previous one, use setValue(previous => ...). Objects and arrays must be replaced with updated copies.

useEffect()

useEffect(setup, dependencies) synchronizes a component with an external system after commit. The setup may return a cleanup function. With no dependency array it runs after every commit; with listed dependencies it resynchronizes when they change; an empty array states that setup uses no reactive dependencies. Cleanup runs before a replacement setup and on unmount.

Do not say “an empty array means guaranteed exactly once.” Development Strict Mode intentionally performs an extra setup/cleanup cycle to reveal broken cleanup. Effects also run again if the component is mounted again.

Example: complete example: start/stop timer

Save as App.jsx in a configured React JSX project.

React · JSX
import {useEffect, useState} from "react";

export default function App() {
  const [seconds, setSeconds] = useState(0);
  const [running, setRunning] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!running) return;
    const timer = window.setInterval(() => {
      setSeconds(previous => previous + 1);
    }, 1000);
    return () => window.clearInterval(timer);
  }, [running]);
  return <main><h1>Timer</h1>
    <p aria-live="polite">Elapsed ticks: {seconds}</p>
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setRunning(true)} disabled={running}>Start</button>
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setRunning(false)} disabled={!running}>Stop</button>
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setSeconds(0)}>Reset</button>
  </main>;
}

Algorithm and working

Initialize elapsed ticks and running flag → when Start changes running to true, effect setup creates one interval → each tick queues an increment → when Stop changes the flag, cleanup clears the previous interval → unmount also clears it. Reset changes the displayed count but does not implicitly change the running flag.

Sample behavior: initially 0; after starting and approximately two timer callbacks, 2; after Stop, it remains 2. Browser scheduling may delay callbacks, especially in background tabs, so this is a tick counter rather than a precision stopwatch.

The effect depends on running. It does not need to capture seconds because the setter uses a functional updater; adding seconds would unnecessarily recreate the interval after each tick. The stable setter itself does not need to be included as a changing dependency.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

Without cleanup, repeated starts/mounts could leave extra intervals. Avoid putting derived arithmetic into an effect when it can be calculated during render. useState manages UI memory; useEffect connects that UI to external behavior. Their correct use depends on call order, snapshots, dependencies and cleanup—not on memorizing an exact one-to-one mapping to class lifecycle methods.

Conclusion: useState manages local memory while useEffect synchronizes external work. The timer demonstrates correct dependencies, cleanup and top-level hook calls rather than side effects during rendering.

Long 37
Question
Explain useState and useMemo hooks with example. …
LongUnit 22.4 Hooks
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: useState stores a value that affects rendering and supplies a setter to request an update. useMemo caches the result of a pure calculation between renders while its dependencies remain unchanged. It is for performance optimization, not for storing essential mutable state or performing effects.

Definitions and differences

Aspect useState useMemo
Syntax [value, setter] = useState(initial) result = useMemo(calculate, deps)
Changes Setter requests a new state/render Recomputed when dependencies change
Purpose Source-of-truth UI memory Avoid repeated expensive derived calculations
Callback purity Initializers/updaters must be pure Calculation must be pure
Reliability role State is part of component semantics Cache may be discarded; not a correctness guarantee

A derived value need not be another state variable. For a cheap expression such as count * 2, calculate it directly; memoization adds complexity and comparison overhead.

Example: complete example

The following App.jsx filters products and totals their prices. The dataset is deliberately small for understanding; a real performance benefit should be confirmed by profiling a larger workload.

React · JSX
import {useMemo, useState} from "react";

const products = [
  {id: 1, name: "Notebook", price: 80},
  {id: 2, name: "Pen", price: 20},
  {id: 3, name: "Web Design Book", price: 300},
  {id: 4, name: "Sketch Book", price: 120}
];
export default function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const [clicks, setClicks] = useState(0);
  const visible = useMemo(() => {
    const term = query.trim().toLowerCase();
    return products.filter(p => p.name.toLowerCase().includes(term));
  }, [query]);
  const total = useMemo(() => {
    return visible.reduce((sum, product) => sum + product.price, 0);
  }, [visible]);
  return <main><h1>Product filter</h1>
    <label>Search <input value={query}
      onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} /></label>
    {visible.length ? <ul>{visible.map(p =>
      <li key={p.id}>{p.name}: ₹{p.price}</li>)}</ul> : <p>No matches.</p>}
    <p>Sum of listed prices: ₹{total}</p>
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setClicks(c => c + 1)}>
      Unrelated clicks: {clicks}
    </button>
  </main>;
}

Algorithm and dependency reasoning

State holds the search query and unrelated click count. The first memo derives a filtered array from the query. Because products is an immutable module-level constant, it is not a changing reactive dependency. If products came from props or state, it would need to be in the dependency array too.

The second memo totals the filtered results and depends on visible. Changing the query can create a new array and recompute the total. Changing only clicks causes a render but leaves the dependencies unchanged, so the cached calculations can be reused. The button still updates normally; memoization does not freeze the whole component.

Sample input and output

With an empty query, all four records appear and the total is ₹520. Searching book returns Notebook, Web Design Book and Sketch Book, with total ₹500. A nonmatching term shows No matches and total ₹0, because reduce has an explicit zero initial value.

Limitations / precautions — edge cases

Dependencies are compared by identity/value using React's comparison; creating a fresh object dependency every render defeats caching unless its construction is reconsidered. Never mutate products behind the memo's back, perform network requests inside useMemo or rely on a calculation running only once. Development checks may call the calculation more than once to detect impurity. State determines behavior; memoization should only make an already-correct calculation cheaper.

Conclusion: useState stores changing data; useMemo caches a calculation result when its dependencies are unchanged. Memoization is an optional optimization, not a replacement for correct state or pure calculations.

Long 38
Question
Explain useRef and useCallback of React.JS. …
LongUnit 22.4 Hooks
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: useRef(initialValue) returns a stable object with a .current property. It can hold a DOM element or another value that must survive renders but does not itself need to trigger UI rendering. Attaching ref={inputRef} to an input makes React set inputRef.current to that node after mounting and clear it on removal.

useRef: stable mutable reference

Common uses include focusing an input, storing a timer identifier and keeping imperative integration handles. Changing .current does not schedule a render; use state for values displayed reactively. Avoid using render-time ref mutation as a substitute for proper state updates.

useCallback: stable function identity

useCallback(function, dependencies) returns a function reference that can be reused while its dependencies remain equal. This is useful when a memoized child receives a callback or an effect legitimately depends on a function. It does not call the function, and it does not mean JavaScript never evaluates a new function expression; React can return the earlier cached reference.

useRef useCallback
Stable mutable container Cached function reference
.current can be changed imperatively New dependency values produce a new callback
Does not itself re-render Does not itself prevent a parent's render
DOM access / nonvisual mutable values Prop identity / dependency optimization

Example: complete example

This React JSX App.jsx combines focus control and a memoized child button.

React · JSX
import {memo, useCallback, useRef, useState} from "react";

const AddButton = memo(function AddButton({onAdd}) {
  return <button type="button" onClick={onAdd}>Add one</button>;
});
export default function App() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const [compact, setCompact] = useState(false);
  const addOne = useCallback(() => {
    setCount(previous => previous + 1);
  }, []);
  function focusName() {
    inputRef.current?.focus();
  }
  return <main style={{padding: compact ? 8 : 24}}>
    <h1>Refs and callbacks</h1>
    <label>Name <input ref={inputRef} value={name}
      onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} /></label>
    <button type="button" onClick={focusName}>Focus name</button>
    <p>Hello, {name || "visitor"}. Count: {count}</p>
    <AddButton onAdd={addOne} />
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setCompact(c => !c)}>Toggle spacing</button>
  </main>;
}

Algorithm, working and output

Create the input ref and state → React attaches the input node → Focus name accesses the mounted node → Add one invokes the cached callback and queues a functional count update → toggling spacing changes unrelated state.

Sample behavior: clicking Focus name moves keyboard focus into the text input. Typing Asha displays Hello, Asha. Clicking Add one twice displays Count: 2. The callback does not capture a stale count because it uses a functional updater; the setter is stable, so the empty dependency array is appropriate in this particular code.

AddButton is wrapped in memo. When the parent changes name or spacing, the onAdd reference remains the same, allowing React to skip that child's unnecessary render. Memoization remains an optimization, not a correctness guarantee. Without a consumer that benefits from stable identity, adding useCallback everywhere can be pointless overhead.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

A ref can be null before mount or after removal, so optional chaining protects imperative access. If a callback reads a changing prop or state value directly, include that value in its dependency list or restructure appropriately; an empty array is not a universal performance shortcut. Use refs for imperative/nonvisual persistence, state for UI memory, and callbacks for measured identity-sensitive optimizations.

Conclusion: useRef stores a persistent mutable reference without triggering rendering, while useCallback stabilizes a returned function identity. Use each for its distinct role and keep dependencies correct.

Unit 3 — Fundamentals of Angular

(5 questions)(5 questions)

3.1 Concepts and characteristics of Angular

Long 39
Question
Explain features of Angular JS in detail. …
LongUnit 33.1 Concepts and characteristics of Angular
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: AngularJS is the original 1.x JavaScript framework for dynamic browser applications. It extends HTML through directives, connects views to models and supplies services such as routing, HTTP and dependency injection. It is not the same framework as modern TypeScript-based Angular. Official AngularJS support ended in January 2022, so the examples here serve the historical syllabus rather than a recommendation for a new production system.

Major features

1. Declarative templates and directives. Attributes such as ng-app, ng-model, ng-repeat and ng-bind attach behavior to HTML. Custom directives can encapsulate reusable UI/DOM integration rather than placing every manipulation in a controller.

2. Data binding. Interpolation and ng-bind display model values. ng-model connects form controls to the model in both directions. AngularJS's digest process evaluates watched expressions and updates the view; it is not the same as React's reconciliation model.

3. MVC/MVVM-style separation. The model stores application data, the view describes presentation and a controller prepares data and actions for the view. $scope is a binding context; controllerAs exposes a controller instance under a named alias and can reduce scope-property confusion.

4. Modules. angular.module("app", [dependencies]) groups controllers, services and other registrations and declares dependencies. Omitting the dependency array retrieves an existing module.

5. Dependency injection and services. Controllers can request $http, $filter or application services by name. The injector supplies them, improving testability and avoiding manually constructed global dependencies. Explicit array annotation is safe when code is minified.

6. Forms and validation. Named controls expose $valid, $invalid, $dirty, $touched and error objects. Directives such as required, ng-minlength and ng-pattern support UI feedback. None of these replaces backend validation.

7. Filters. Expressions can format data using currency, date, uppercase, number and other filters. Formatting is distinct from changing the stored model.

8. Routing and HTTP. The optional ngRoute module maps URLs to templates/controllers through $routeProvider and ng-view. $http communicates with backend APIs and returns promises.

9. Testability and reusable abstractions. Injection and separated services allow dependencies to be replaced in tests. Directives and components encapsulate behavior, although excessive watchers or tangled scopes can make a large application hard to maintain.

Example: working example

Save as an HTML file beside a trusted local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js. The library is a prerequisite for running this example, not a dependency of the question-bank reader.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="billApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>AngularJS features</title></head>
<body ng-controller="BillController as vm">
  <h1>{{vm.title}}</h1>
  <label>Quantity <input type="number" min="1" step="1" ng-model="vm.qty"></label>
  <p>Unit price: {{vm.price | currency:'₹':2}}</p>
  <p>Total: {{vm.total() | currency:'₹':2}}</p>
  <ul><li ng-repeat="item in vm.features track by item">{{item}}</li></ul>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module("billApp", []).controller("BillController", function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.title = "Bill calculator";
      vm.qty = 2;
      vm.price = 50;
      vm.features = ["Binding", "Controller", "Filter", "Directive"];
      vm.total = function() {
        return typeof vm.qty === "number" && vm.qty >= 1 ? vm.qty * vm.price : 0;
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Algorithm and result

Bootstrap billApp → construct the controller → bind its alias to the template → update quantity from the input → evaluate the total → format currency and repeat the feature list. Initially the total is ₹100.00 with the standard en-US locale; changing quantity to 3 produces ₹150.00. The currency filter formats the number but does not perform currency conversion.

Limitations

Digest/watch overhead, complex inherited scopes and legacy maintenance requirements are important limitations. Business logic belongs in testable controllers/services rather than large expressions or ng-init. AngularJS offered integrated declarative web-app features, but modern Angular uses a distinct component/compiler architecture and must not be described using AngularJS APIs interchangeably.

Conclusion: AngularJS integrated directives, binding, controllers, services, filters and forms into a browser framework. These are legacy 1.x concepts and must remain separate from modern Angular terminology.

Long 40
Question
Explain Angular Architecture with neat diagram. …
LongUnit 33.1 Concepts and characteristics of Angular
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: This answer interprets Angular Architecture as modern Angular (2+). AngularJS architecture is different and is contrasted at the end. The example uses an Angular 17-style standalone application, which supports the syllabus's classic directives without implying that these are the newest recommended control-flow forms.

Ambiguity note: “Angular” is interpreted as modern Angular here. The diagram and TypeScript program use a stated Angular 17-style setup; AngularJS 1.x APIs are contrasted rather than mixed into the same architecture.

Scope and architectural idea

Angular structures an application as a tree of components. Templates describe views; component classes hold view-related logic; services handle reusable responsibilities; dependency injection supplies services; and change detection keeps bound views synchronized with application state.

Labelled architecture diagram

The component tree controls presentation. The injector graph supplies dependencies and is not identical to the DOM tree. HttpClient talks to a backend; Angular does not directly replace the database server.

Main architectural building blocks

  1. Components: a class plus @Component metadata, including selector, template and styles. They own a focused part of the interface.
  2. Templates and bindings: interpolation ({{x}}), property binding ([disabled]), event binding ((click)) and two-way binding ([(ngModel)]) connect data and events.
  3. Directives: extend element behavior; classic structural directives create embedded views, while attribute directives alter behavior/appearance.
  4. Pipes: transform displayed values, such as date or currency formatting, without inherently changing source data.
  5. Services and DI: reusable business/data logic belongs in services; providers tell injectors how to supply values or instances.
  6. Routing: @angular/router maps URLs to views displayed by a router outlet, supporting navigation without full document reloads.
  7. Forms and HTTP: Angular offers template-driven/reactive forms and an Observable-based HTTP client.
  8. Compilation and change detection: templates are compiled, events/data changes are processed, and affected bindings are checked and rendered.

Standalone components and NgModules

A standalone component explicitly imports the components, directives and pipes used by its template. bootstrapApplication can start it. Traditional NgModules instead organize declarations, imports, providers and bootstrap components through @NgModule; standalone and module-based code can interoperate. Angular's NgModule is not AngularJS's angular.module API.

Example: complete minimal main.ts

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project with its normal polyfills and an index page containing <app-root></app-root>.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component, Injectable, inject} from '@angular/core';
import {CommonModule} from '@angular/common';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';

@Injectable({providedIn: 'root'})
class CourseService {
  getCourses(): string[] { return ['MongoDB', 'React', 'Angular']; }
}
@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [CommonModule],
  template: `<h1>Courses</h1>
    <ul><li *ngFor="let course of courses">{{course}}</li></ul>`,
  styles: ['h1 { color: #176b5b; }']
})
class AppComponent {
  courses = inject(CourseService).getCourses();
}
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Working, output

Bootstrapping creates the root component; its injector resolves CourseService; the component receives an array; *ngFor creates three list items; interpolation displays MongoDB, React and Angular. The service is easy to substitute in tests, while the template focuses on presentation.

In AngularJS, equivalent discussions involve angular.module, controllers, $scope, the digest cycle and ng-view; those names must not be inserted into a modern Angular architecture diagram as if they were the same APIs. Modern Angular's architecture emphasizes component composition, compiled templates, dependency injection and clear separation between browser UI and backend services.

Limitations / precautions

Import the template features and register the providers actually used by the application. A missing provider or missing standalone import prevents the intended component behavior. Keep heavy repeated calculations out of frequently checked bindings, and enforce data permissions in the backend rather than relying on route visibility.

Conclusion: Modern Angular composes a UI from components, compiled templates, services and injectors. Routing, forms and HTTP extend that architecture without replacing a backend or equating the injector tree with the DOM.

3.1.1.2 Modules & dependency injection

Long 41
Question
⭐⭐⭐ What is a module in AngularJS? Explain how to create a controller of the module with an example. …
LongUnit 33.1.1.2 Modules & dependency injection★ × 3
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: An AngularJS module is a named container for application registrations such as controllers, directives, services, filters and configuration. It also declares dependencies on other modules. It is not a JavaScript ES module, and it is not modern Angular's @NgModule class.

Definition of an AngularJS module

Creation: angular.module('myApp', []). The second argument is the dependency array; ['ngRoute'] would request the routing module. Retrieval: angular.module('myApp') without the second argument returns the existing module. Accidentally calling creation again can reset the module's registrations.

Controller and scope

A controller initializes view data and supplies actions. It should not perform arbitrary DOM manipulation; use directives for DOM integration and services for reusable business/data logic. The injected $scope exposes properties to the linked template. Alternatively, ng-controller="StudentController as vm" can expose an instance alias and reduce implicit scope lookup.

Algorithm

Create the module → register a controller using dependency annotation → initialize a student object → attach a full-name function → load the library/module code → bootstrap through ng-app → bind the controller through ng-controller → let inputs and expressions update the view.

Example: complete working example

Save the following HTML beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="studentApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Module and controller</title></head>
<body ng-controller="StudentController">
  <h1>{{title}}</h1>
  <label>First name <input ng-model="student.firstName"></label>
  <label>Last name <input ng-model="student.lastName"></label>
  <p>Hello {{fullName()}}</p>
  <p>Course: <span ng-bind="student.course"></span></p>
  <button type="button" ng-click="reset()">Reset</button>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    var app = angular.module('studentApp', []);
    app.controller('StudentController', ['$scope', function($scope) {
      $scope.title = 'Student profile';
      $scope.student = {firstName: 'Robert', lastName: 'Desoza', course: 'BCA'};
      $scope.fullName = function() {
        return ($scope.student.firstName + ' ' + $scope.student.lastName).trim();
      };
      $scope.reset = function() {
        $scope.student.firstName = 'Robert';
        $scope.student.lastName = 'Desoza';
      };
    }]);
  </script>
</body></html>

Explanation of important lines

ng-app="studentApp" identifies the application root and module name. The browser must load AngularJS and register the module before automatic bootstrapping completes. ng-controller="StudentController" creates a controller instance and a linked child scope for that region.

The array ['$scope', function($scope) {...}] makes the dependency name explicit. A minifier can rename the function parameter without breaking the string-based dependency declaration. The student object keeps related fields together and avoids some primitive-property shadowing problems when nested scopes are introduced.

ng-model connects editable fields to the object. Interpolation calls a small, side-effect-free function to produce the greeting, and ng-bind writes course text. Avoid expensive or state-changing functions in watched expressions because AngularJS may evaluate them repeatedly during digest checks.

Limitations / precautions — sample output and edge cases

Initially the page shows Hello Robert Desoza and Course: BCA. Changing the first field to Asha immediately displays Hello Asha Desoza. Reset restores the original names. A missing module registration or a mismatch between studentApp and ng-app prevents proper bootstrapping; a missing library leaves bindings unevaluated.

Conclusion: A module organizes the application and its dependencies; a controller prepares the view's data/actions. This separation improves reuse and testing, while binding updates presentation. AngularJS is legacy technology with ended official support, so the pattern should be understood in its 1.x context.

Long 42
Question
Describe Dependency Injection in Angular with example diagram. …
LongUnit 33.1.1.2 Modules & dependency injection
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern in which a class receives required dependencies from an external mechanism rather than constructing them directly. In modern Angular, providers describe how to create/provide values, and injectors resolve requests identified by tokens. This separates a consumer from a specific implementation and makes testing easier.

Labelled diagram

A provider does not mean “make a new instance on every method call.” An injector generally caches a service instance for its provider. Scope matters: a root provider is shared in the root environment, while a provider on a component can create a separate instance for that component's subtree.

Main DI concepts

Concept Meaning
Consumer Component/service requesting a dependency
Token Lookup key, such as a class or InjectionToken
Provider Instruction such as useClass, useValue, useFactory or useExisting
Injector Resolves tokens using its own and ancestor providers
@Injectable Metadata used for an injectable class and optional provision scope
inject() / constructor injection Ways to request dependencies in an allowed injection context

An interface disappears at runtime, so use an explicit InjectionToken when a TypeScript interface is the abstraction to inject. Calling inject() in an arbitrary later event handler is not an allowed injection context; obtain the dependency during construction/field initialization and then use it later.

Example: complete modern Angular example

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project with <app-root> in index.html; replace src/main.ts with this educational standalone example.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component, Injectable, inject} from '@angular/core';
import {CommonModule} from '@angular/common';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';

@Injectable({providedIn: 'root'})
class CourseService {
  getCourses(): string[] { return ['HTML', 'React', 'MongoDB']; }
  count(): number { return this.getCourses().length; }
}
@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [CommonModule],
  template: `<h1>Injected courses</h1>
    <p>Total: {{total}}</p>
    <ul><li *ngFor="let course of courses">{{course}}</li></ul>`
})
class AppComponent {
  private courseService = inject(CourseService);
  courses = this.courseService.getCourses();
  total = this.courseService.count();
}
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Algorithm, working and result

Register CourseService in the root injector → bootstrap the component → resolve its inject(CourseService) request → supply the service → call its methods → bind the returned data. Output: Total: 3, followed by HTML, React and MongoDB. AppComponent never executes new CourseService() itself.

Constructor injection, for example a constructor parameter typed as CourseService with a private modifier, is an alternative to inject. In a test, the provider can be overridden with a fake returning a known list; the component need not know whether data came from a server or a test fixture.

Limitations / precautions — benefits, limitations

DI reduces tight coupling, supports shared services, centralizes construction and makes tests more focused. Missing providers can cause injection errors; circular dependencies can also fail and often indicate poor separation of responsibilities. Shared services must not accidentally leak one user's state across inappropriate scopes.

AngularJS also has dependency injection, but uses string-named services, factories and annotations such as ['$http', function($http) {...}]. Do not mix those syntax forms with modern Angular's class/token-based examples. DI is an architectural mechanism for supplying collaborators, not merely a synonym for importing a file.

Conclusion: Dependency injection connects a consumer to a registered provider through a token and injector. Deliberate provider scope improves reuse, substitution in tests and control of instance lifetime.

3.2 Routing and navigation

Long 43
Question
⭐ Explain $routeProvider service from ngRoute of AngularJS. …
LongUnit 33.2 Routing and navigation★ × 1
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: $routeProvider is the configuration provider of AngularJS's optional ngRoute module. It maps URL paths to route definitions containing a template, controller and optional resolution rules. It is injected into a module's .config(...) function; the runtime routing service is $route, and route parameters are exposed through $routeParams.

Ambiguity note: The source calls $routeProvider a service. It is a configuration-time provider in AngularJS ngRoute; $route is a related runtime service.

Definition and setup

Load local, matching-version angular.min.js and angular-route.min.js, then declare ['ngRoute']. The selected view appears inside ng-view, not modern Angular's <router-outlet>.

Important API elements

Element Purpose
.when('/path', definition) Register a route
template / templateUrl Inline markup or template location/cache key
controller / controllerAs View logic and optional alias
:id in the path Parameter captured into $routeParams.id
resolve Dependencies/data that must resolve before route activation
.otherwise({redirectTo: ...}) Fallback for unmatched routes

Route order and specificity matter. Configuration does not automatically enforce authentication; backend APIs must authorize requests regardless of which view is visible.

Algorithm

Bootstrap the module → configure hash routing and routes → create navigation links → listen for URL changes → match a path → instantiate its controller → insert the template into ng-view → update route parameters as navigation occurs.

Example: complete example

Serve this HTML and the two local libraries with a simple local static server. Templates are embedded in AngularJS's template cache, so no external template files are needed.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="routeApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>ngRoute example</title></head>
<body>
  <nav><a href="#!/home">Home</a> | <a href="#!/student/7">Student 7</a></nav>
  <main ng-view></main>
  <script type="text/ng-template" id="home.html">
    <h1>Home</h1><p>Choose a student from the navigation.</p>
  </script>
  <script type="text/ng-template" id="student.html">
    <h1>Student</h1><p>Selected student ID: {{studentId}}</p>
  </script>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script src="angular-route.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('routeApp', ['ngRoute'])
      .config(['$routeProvider', '$locationProvider', function(routes, location) {
        location.hashPrefix('!');
        routes.when('/home', {templateUrl: 'home.html'})
          .when('/student/:id', {
            templateUrl: 'student.html', controller: 'StudentController'
          })
          .otherwise({redirectTo: '/home'});
      }])
      .controller('StudentController', ['$scope', '$routeParams', function(scope, params) {
        scope.studentId = params.id;
      }]);
  </script>
</body></html>

Explanation and sample output

Hash prefix ! makes the link #!/student/7 correspond to route path /student/7. The :id placeholder captures the string "7". The controller exposes it on scope, and the cached template displays Selected student ID: 7. The Home link displays the home heading, and an unknown path redirects to /home.

The script tag with type="text/ng-template" is a template definition, not an executed JavaScript program. Its ID must match templateUrl. Array-style injection prevents minification from breaking dependency names even though local parameter names differ.

Limitations / precautions — error handling

A missing ngRoute script/module prevents the provider from being available. A wrong template path causes template-loading failure; a rejected resolve leads to a route error that the application should handle. Validate and authorize any route ID before using it in backend operations. Hash routing avoids many server fallback issues; HTML5 history mode needs appropriate server routing configuration. $routeProvider coordinates a legacy SPA's views, while actual security remains a server responsibility.

Conclusion: $routeProvider defines AngularJS path-to-view rules during configuration. ng-view displays the active template, while routing parameters and backend permissions still require explicit validation.

4.1 Angular core features & lifecycle hooks

Long 44
Question
Explain Angular Lifecycle Hooks with examples. …
LongUnit 44.1 Angular core features & lifecycle hooks
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: A modern Angular component has a lifecycle from creation through input changes, view/content checks and destruction. Implement named hook methods to perform work at appropriate stages. This is the Angular 2+ API, not AngularJS's $onInit component API. The example targets Angular 17-style standalone components and classic *ngIf.

Ambiguity note: These unprefixed lifecycle hook names belong to modern Angular. AngularJS component hooks use names such as $onInit and are not interchangeable with this sequence.

Hooks and purposes

Hook When it runs Suitable work
ngOnChanges(changes) When Angular updates bound inputs Respond to current/previous input values
ngOnInit() Once after initial inputs are set Initialize input-dependent state or start work
ngDoCheck() Whenever this component is checked Carefully designed custom checking
ngAfterContentInit() Once after projected content initializes Access initialized content queries
ngAfterContentChecked() After projected content is checked Rare lightweight post-content checks
ngAfterViewInit() Once after the component's view initializes Access initialized view queries
ngAfterViewChecked() After the component's view is checked Rare lightweight post-view checks
ngOnDestroy() Just before destruction Remove listeners, timers and subscriptions

The constructor is a JavaScript construction step, not one of these lifecycle hook methods. During first initialization, ngOnChanges (when inputs are assigned) precedes ngOnInit, then checking/content/view hooks follow. Checked hooks can run frequently; do not use them as places for expensive polling or unconditional state updates.

Sequence diagram

Modern Angular also provides render callbacks such as afterNextRender; these are functions with a different scope from the instance hook methods in the table. They should not be confused with ngAfterViewInit.

Example: complete illustrative main.ts

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project, its usual polyfills and <app-root> in index.html.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component, Input, OnChanges, OnInit, DoCheck, AfterContentInit,
  AfterContentChecked, AfterViewInit, AfterViewChecked, OnDestroy,
  SimpleChanges} from '@angular/core';
import {CommonModule} from '@angular/common';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';

@Component({selector: 'life-child', standalone: true,
  template: `<p>Child label: {{label}}</p><ng-content></ng-content>`})
class LifeChild implements OnChanges, OnInit, DoCheck, AfterContentInit,
  AfterContentChecked, AfterViewInit, AfterViewChecked, OnDestroy {
  @Input() label = '';
  private timer: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | undefined;
  ngOnChanges(changes: SimpleChanges) { console.log('changes', changes['label']); }
  ngOnInit() {
    console.log('init');
    this.timer = setInterval(() => console.log('background tick'), 5000);
  }
  ngDoCheck() { console.log('check'); }
  ngAfterContentInit() { console.log('content initialized'); }
  ngAfterContentChecked() { console.log('content checked'); }
  ngAfterViewInit() { console.log('view initialized'); }
  ngAfterViewChecked() { console.log('view checked'); }
  ngOnDestroy() { clearInterval(this.timer); console.log('destroy'); }
}
@Component({selector: 'app-root', standalone: true,
  imports: [CommonModule, LifeChild],
  template: `<button (click)="label = label + '!'">Change input</button>
    <button (click)="visible = !visible">Toggle child</button>
    <life-child *ngIf="visible" [label]="label"><em>Projected content</em></life-child>`})
class AppComponent { label = 'Hello'; visible = true; }
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Working and expected observations

Initially the child shows Hello, followed by projected content; the console records initialization hooks in lifecycle order. Clicking Change input produces an input-change record and the label becomes Hello!, but ngOnInit does not run again for that same instance. Hiding the child triggers ngOnDestroy, which clears its interval. Showing it again creates a new instance and runs initialization hooks again.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

Actual check counts can vary with the application and development checks, so do not assume one console message per user click. Avoid changing already-checked bound state in after-view/content hooks; this can cause consistency errors or loops. Lifecycle knowledge is most useful for placing input-dependent initialization, DOM access and cleanup correctly rather than treating every hook as a compulsory method.

Conclusion: Angular lifecycle hooks run at defined input, initialization, checking, view and destruction stages. Select the hook that matches the work and avoid treating every hook as a safe place to change bound state.

Long 45
Question
Differentiate between ngOnChanges, ngOnInit, and ngDoCheck. …
LongUnit 44.1 Angular core features & lifecycle hooks
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: ngOnChanges, ngOnInit and ngDoCheck are modern Angular lifecycle hooks. They solve different problems: reacting to input assignment, initializing an instance and performing custom checks. They are not interchangeable names for “runs when data changes.”

Ambiguity note: This comparison uses modern Angular lifecycle interfaces. “Changes” means input changes detected by Angular, not an automatic deep comparison of every mutated object.

Comparison table

Basis ngOnChanges ngOnInit ngDoCheck
Trigger Angular detects a bound input change Initial component setup after inputs Every check of this component
Frequency Initially and for subsequent input changes Once per instance Potentially frequent
Arguments SimpleChanges map None None
First-run order Before ngOnInit, if there are input changes Before first ngDoCheck After changes/init in initial cycle
Typical purpose Recompute from changed inputs Initialize from inputs / start work Detect a custom difference not captured automatically
Does it automatically deep-diff objects? No No No; custom logic is the developer's responsibility
Main risk Assuming nested mutation gives a new input reference Expecting it on every update Expensive or state-changing checks causing overhead/loops

SimpleChange gives previousValue, currentValue and firstChange, plus an isFirstChange() method. A bound object/array can keep the same reference when its contents are mutated; that may not trigger ngOnChanges even though another check occurs.

Example: complete demonstration

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project with standard polyfills and <app-root>. Default change detection is assumed, not an OnPush configuration.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component, Input, OnChanges, OnInit, DoCheck, SimpleChanges} from '@angular/core';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';

@Component({selector: 'items-child', standalone: true,
  template: `<p>Items: {{items.join(', ')}}</p>`})
class ItemsChild implements OnChanges, OnInit, DoCheck {
  @Input() items: string[] = [];
  private previousLength = 0;
  ngOnChanges(changes: SimpleChanges) {
    if (changes['items']) console.log('Input reference changed', changes['items']);
  }
  ngOnInit() {
    this.previousLength = this.items.length;
    console.log('Initialized once with', this.previousLength, 'items');
  }
  ngDoCheck() {
    if (this.items.length !== this.previousLength) {
      console.log('Length changed to', this.items.length);
      this.previousLength = this.items.length;
    }
  }
}
@Component({selector: 'app-root', standalone: true, imports: [ItemsChild],
  template: `<button (click)="mutate()">Mutate existing array</button>
    <button (click)="replace()">Replace array</button>
    <items-child [items]="items"></items-child>`})
class AppComponent {
  items = ['HTML'];
  mutate() { this.items.push('CSS'); }
  replace() { this.items = [...this.items, 'React']; }
}
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Algorithm and sample behavior

Initialize the parent array → assign it to the child → record initial input change → initialize the previous-length snapshot → compare length during later checks. Initially the child shows HTML and logs initialization once.

Clicking Mutate existing array adds CSS without replacing the array reference. Under the stated default-checking setup, the event leads to a check, ngDoCheck detects the new length, and the view shows HTML, CSS. This mutation does not by itself constitute a new reference for ngOnChanges.

Clicking Replace array creates a new array containing React. The child receives a different input reference, so ngOnChanges reports it and the custom length check can also report the longer length. ngOnInit still does not repeat for the same child instance.

Limitations

The custom checker detects only length changes, not replacement of one element by another at the same length. A full differ would need a more deliberate strategy; repeatedly serializing large objects in ngDoCheck is usually poor design. Immutable updates often simplify detection and work better with optimized change detection. Use each hook for its intended responsibility rather than relying on it as a universal deep-change observer.

Conclusion: ngOnChanges reacts to detected input changes, ngOnInit performs one-time initialization, and ngDoCheck supports custom checking. Their different triggers and costs determine the appropriate choice.

4.2 Angular directives & component communication

Long 46
Question
What is DOM? Explain Directives in detail. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: The Document Object Model (DOM) is the browser's object-tree representation of a document. HTML elements, attributes and text are represented through nodes and related interfaces. JavaScript can read, create, update or remove nodes, and user events propagate through the tree. The DOM is an API and live structure, not the original HTML file as a plain string.

Ambiguity note: The topic mixes a general browser concept with framework directives. The main directive explanation uses AngularJS 1.x, then explicitly distinguishes modern Angular.

DOM: definition and structure

A framework manages parts of this tree from application data. Directly changing framework-owned nodes can conflict with its later updates, so use the framework's binding/directive mechanisms where possible.

AngularJS directives

In the surrounding syllabus context, a directive is an AngularJS marker on an HTML element that tells its compiler to attach behavior, create views or connect data. AngularJS compiles the template, recognizes directives and links them to scope values. This answer uses AngularJS 1.8.x; modern Angular directives have a different API.

Directive Function
ng-app Identifies the automatically bootstrapped root/module
ng-controller Associates a controller and scope with a region
ng-model Connects an editable control to a model and validation
ng-bind Writes a model expression as text
ng-repeat Repeats a template for collection items
ng-if Creates/removes a conditional block
ng-show / ng-hide Toggles visibility while retaining DOM nodes
ng-class Applies classes based on an expression

Built-in and custom directive forms

AngularJS custom directives use .directive(name, factory). The factory returns a directive definition object. Important fields include restrict, template/templateUrl, scope, controller and link. restrict can include element (E), attribute (A), class (C) and legacy comment (M) matching. Element and attribute forms are normally clearer than class/comment forms.

A camelCase registration such as welcomeCard appears as kebab-case <welcome-card> in HTML. An isolated scope helps a reusable directive avoid accidental dependence on its surrounding scope. Direct DOM event integration belongs in a link/directive integration layer and should be cleaned up on destruction.

Example: complete example

Place this HTML beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="directiveApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>DOM and directives</title></head>
<body ng-controller="PageController as vm">
  <label>Name <input ng-model="vm.name"></label>
  <welcome-card name="vm.name"></welcome-card>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('directiveApp', [])
      .controller('PageController', function() { this.name = 'Asha'; })
      .directive('welcomeCard', function() {
        return {
          restrict: 'E',
          scope: {name: '<'},
          template: '<article><h2 ng-bind="name"></h2><p>Custom directive card</p></article>'
        };
      });
  </script>
</body></html>

Algorithm and output

Bootstrap the module → create PageController → bind the input to vm.name → match the custom element → create its isolated binding → render the directive template → update text when the parent's name changes. Initial output: a card headed Asha. Typing Ravi changes the card heading to Ravi. The < binding is AngularJS 1.5+ one-way input binding; the directive does not write back to the parent's property.

Modern Angular distinction

Modern Angular uses @Directive and @Component, property/event bindings and dependency injection, not .directive()/restrict/$scope. A component is a directive with its own template in modern Angular terminology. In both systems, directives connect declarative UI instructions to behavior, reducing scattered manual DOM operations. Never compile untrusted strings as templates, and remember that hiding a DOM node is not access control.

Limitations / precautions

Do not let unrelated code and directives compete to rewrite the same DOM subtree. Custom directives should release listeners or other resources when destroyed. Compile only trusted templates: AngularJS expressions and raw HTML integration must not become a path for executing untrusted template content.

Conclusion: The DOM is the browser's document tree; AngularJS directives attach template behavior to elements in that tree. Framework version and directive scope determine the correct APIs and lifecycle rules.

Long 47
Question
Explain ng-app, ng-model and ng-bind directive with example. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: ng-app, ng-model and ng-bind are AngularJS 1.x directives with distinct responsibilities: bootstrapping, editable model binding and text display. They work together, but none replaces the others.

Purpose of the three directives

Directive Typical syntax Responsibility
ng-app ng-app="profileApp" Select the root and module for automatic bootstrap
ng-model ng-model="vm.name" Synchronize a form control with a model value
ng-bind ng-bind="vm.name" Set element text from an expression

ng-app in detail

Place ng-app on a root element such as <html> or a container. AngularJS locates it when the document is ready and starts the named module. The framework script and module definition must already be loaded. Do not nest multiple automatically bootstrapped applications or assume adding ng-app also downloads AngularJS; manual bootstrapping is a separate advanced technique.

ng-model in detail

ng-model primarily connects inputs, textareas and selects to the model. User changes are parsed/validated and written into the model; model changes are formatted back to the control. It also participates in form state such as $dirty, $touched and $invalid. Use an object path such as vm.name rather than scattered primitive scope values when working with nested scopes.

ng-bind in detail

ng-bind evaluates an expression and replaces the element's text content. The expression appears directly in the attribute; do not write ng-bind="{{vm.name}}". It provides one-way display and does not make a paragraph editable. Unlike raw HTML injection, it does not interpret a supplied string as markup.

Example: complete example and algorithm

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js. Algorithm: create the module/controller → bootstrap → initialize the name → synchronize edits → display the resulting text.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="profileApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Three AngularJS directives</title></head>
<body ng-controller="ProfileController as vm">
  <h1>Profile</h1>
  <label>Name <input type="text" ng-model="vm.name"></label>
  <p>Current name: <span ng-bind="vm.name"></span></p>
  <button type="button" ng-click="vm.name = 'Robert'">Reset</button>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('profileApp', [])
      .controller('ProfileController', function() { this.name = 'Robert'; });
  </script>
</body></html>

Working and sample output

Initially the input contains Robert and the paragraph reads Current name: Robert. Typing Asha updates the model through ng-model; AngularJS's digest/binding mechanism updates the ng-bind span to Asha. Pressing Reset changes the model in the other direction, restoring both the input and span to Robert.

The span is empty in the original HTML before AngularJS runs, so it avoids showing raw {{...}} interpolation text in that location during startup. A missing library or module prevents the application from functioning; it does not make the attribute a native HTML feature.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

A password field bound with ng-model should not be echoed through ng-bind in a real application. Rendering text safely is different from validating or authorizing the underlying data. These directives belong to AngularJS; modern Angular uses bootstrapping APIs and bindings such as [(ngModel)], not ng-app and ng-bind. The example cleanly separates application startup, editable state and text output.

Conclusion: ng-app identifies the AngularJS application, ng-model connects an editable control and ng-bind displays a value as text. Together they support a small, clearly owned binding cycle.

Long 48
Question
⭐ Write about ng-app, ng-init and ng-repeat directives of AngularJS. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication★ × 1
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: AngularJS directives extend HTML with application behavior. ng-app starts the application region, ng-init evaluates initial expressions in a scope, and ng-repeat creates repeated instances of a template from a collection. The combination can demonstrate a small data-driven table without manually appending DOM rows.

ng-app

ng-app="courseApp" identifies the module for automatic bootstrapping. Create that module with angular.module('courseApp', []) and load AngularJS. The directive belongs on an application root, not on each repeated row. Automatic bootstrapping should not be confused with module creation: both the module definition and the root marker are needed.

ng-init

ng-init="expression" evaluates initialization code in the current scope. For example, ng-init="count=3" introduces a value used by later bindings. It is useful for simple demonstrations, but real datasets, requests and business logic normally belong in controllers/services rather than long HTML expressions.

ng-repeat

ng-repeat="item in items track by item.id" instantiates a template for each array item, with a child scope for each repeated block. track by gives stable identity. Locals such as $index, $first, $last, $middle, $even and $odd describe the current position.

Do not use random tracking values, and do not assume $index is a stable record identity when rows can be reordered. Duplicate tracking keys cause errors. Repeating primitive duplicate values may require an explicit tracking policy, but using an index can preserve the wrong DOM identity after reorder.

Example: complete example

Place the file beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="courseApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Course table</title></head>
<body ng-init="courses=[{id:1,name:'MongoDB',hours:12},{id:2,name:'React',hours:18},{id:3,name:'Angular',hours:16}]">
  <h1>Web designing courses</h1>
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th scope="col">No.</th><th scope="col">Course</th><th scope="col">Hours</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr ng-repeat="course in courses track by course.id">
        <td>{{$index + 1}}</td><td>{{course.name}}</td><td>{{course.hours}}</td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
  <p>Total courses: {{courses.length}}</p>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>angular.module('courseApp', []);</script>
</body></html>

Algorithm and expected result

Bootstrap courseApp → evaluate the array initialization → repeat a row for each object → interpolate its fields → display the array length. The table contains 1 MongoDB 12, 2 React 18, 3 Angular 16, and the paragraph shows Total courses: 3.

The id values are identifiers, while $index + 1 is a display sequence. If the array is reordered, the visible sequence changes but stable IDs allow AngularJS to associate each row with the same record. An empty array produces no data rows and length zero; provide an explicit empty state in a larger application.

Limitations

Large repeated collections create many nodes/watchers and may need pagination or other rendering strategies. Keep repeated expressions simple and avoid repeated network calls in templates. ng-init does not substitute for a controller architecture, and ng-app does not itself supply initial data. Together the three directives illustrate startup, initialization and collection-based rendering, each with a separate role.

Conclusion: ng-app establishes the application region, ng-init evaluates limited initialization and ng-repeat creates repeated views. Stable tracking and controller-owned business data make larger examples maintainable.

Long 49
Question
Explain with an example the AngularJS directives ng-app, ng-init, ng-controller, ng-model, ng-repeat, ng-class and ng-bind. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: The seven requested AngularJS directives cover application startup, initialization, controller attachment, input binding, repetition, conditional classes and text display. The following example shows them together in a small searchable student list. It uses AngularJS 1.8.x, not modern Angular syntax.

Overview and roles

Directive Role in the example
ng-app Bootstrap module studentListApp
ng-init Initialize a small view-local help message
ng-controller Attach StudentController as vm
ng-model Bind a search input to vm.search
ng-repeat Render filtered student records
ng-class Highlight students with marks at least 80
ng-bind Display the heading/help text safely as text

Algorithm

Load/register the application → construct controller data → initialize the help text → render the repeated list → on typing, update the search model → apply the filter → update matching rows and their classes. A local library file is the only runtime prerequisite for this separate example.

Example: complete program

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="studentListApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Directive demonstration</title>
  <style>.honour {background:#e3f4e9;font-weight:bold;} td,th {padding:8px;}</style>
</head>
<body ng-controller="StudentController as vm"
      ng-init="help='Type a name to filter the students.'">
  <h1 ng-bind="vm.title"></h1>
  <p ng-bind="help"></p>
  <label>Search name <input ng-model="vm.search"></label>
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th scope="col">Name</th><th scope="col">Marks</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr ng-repeat="student in vm.students | filter:{name:vm.search} track by student.id"
          ng-class="{'honour': student.marks >= 80}">
        <td ng-bind="student.name"></td><td>{{student.marks}}</td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('studentListApp', []).controller('StudentController', function() {
      this.title = 'Student results';
      this.search = '';
      this.students = [
        {id: 1, name: 'Asha', marks: 82},
        {id: 2, name: 'Ravi', marks: 70},
        {id: 3, name: 'Mira', marks: 91}
      ];
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js. The filter expression is a built-in AngularJS filter used to support the demonstration; it does not modify the original students array.

Explanation of important lines

ng-app matches the name passed to angular.module. ng-controller exposes the controller instance as vm, providing a clear owner for its data. Actual student records are initialized in the controller; ng-init is limited to a small presentation message so it is demonstrated without encouraging business logic in markup.

ng-model synchronizes the search string. ng-repeat iterates over records matching the object's name property. The track by student.id clause comes after the filter and supplies stable identity. Each row gets its own student binding; it does not overwrite a global variable.

ng-class evaluates an object whose class-name key is enabled when its value is truthy. It adds/removes honour as the condition changes instead of replacing all classes unconditionally. ng-bind takes the raw expression student.name, not {{student.name}}, and renders text rather than HTML markup.

Sample output and checks

Initially all three students appear; Asha (82) and Mira (91) are highlighted, while Ravi (70) is not. Typing ravi shows only Ravi through the filter's ordinary case-insensitive matching behavior. Clearing the input restores all records. A nonmatching name leaves no rows; a production UI can add an explicit “no matches” message.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

Keep tracking IDs unique, avoid expensive expressions in repeated rows, and use a controller/service for real initialization. Never use a visibility or class directive as authorization. This one example demonstrates all seven directives while preserving a clear separation between module startup, model ownership and view behavior.

Conclusion: Each directive in the example has a distinct role in bootstrapping, initialization, controller linkage, editing, repetition, styling or display. Combining them works best when logic and data ownership stay explicit.

Long 50
Question
Write short note on HTML DOM directives of AngularJS. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: In AngularJS, HTML DOM directives are commonly taught as directives that control an element's presence, visibility, enabled state, classes or styles based on the model. They reduce the need for scattered manual calls to style.display, classList or removeChild. AngularJS evaluates the associated expressions during its binding/digest process.

Important directives

Directive Effect Important distinction
ng-show Shows when expression is truthy Keeps the element and scope in the DOM
ng-hide Hides when expression is truthy Inverse condition of ng-show
ng-if Creates/removes a block Destroys/recreates its child scope
ng-disabled Controls a supported control's disabled property Use a Boolean expression, not string interpolation
ng-readonly Controls read-only state where supported Read-only differs from disabled
ng-class Adds/removes classes Can use string, array or condition object
ng-style Applies an expression's style object Prefer classes for reusable styling
ng-switch Selects among alternative blocks Used with case/default directives
ng-href / ng-src Defers interpolated URL assignment appropriately Not a licence to use untrusted URLs

A disabled control normally does not participate in native form submission. A read-only supported input remains focusable/submittable, but cannot be edited normally. A plain HTML boolean attribute such as disabled="false" is still present and therefore disables the element; use the directive to control the actual condition.

Example: complete demonstration

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="domApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>DOM directives</title>
  <style>.ready {color:green;} .waiting {color:#8b4d00;}</style>
</head>
<body ng-controller="DomController as vm">
  <label><input type="checkbox" ng-model="vm.agreed"> I agree</label>
  <button type="button" ng-disabled="!vm.agreed" ng-click="vm.message='Accepted'">Continue</button>
  <p ng-class="{ready:vm.agreed, waiting:!vm.agreed}" ng-bind="vm.message"></p>
  <label><input type="checkbox" ng-model="vm.visible"> Show help</label>
  <p ng-show="vm.visible">This help remains in the DOM when hidden.</p>
  <p ng-hide="vm.visible">Help is currently hidden.</p>
  <div ng-if="vm.visible"><input aria-label="Temporary note" placeholder="Destroyed when help is removed"></div>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('domApp', []).controller('DomController', function() {
      this.agreed = false;
      this.visible = false;
      this.message = 'Waiting for agreement';
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Algorithm and observed behavior

Initialize Boolean state → bind checkboxes → evaluate disabled/visibility/class expressions → update the DOM when the user toggles a checkbox. Initially Continue is disabled, the waiting message is shown, the help paragraph is hidden, and the temporary note input does not exist.

Checking I agree enables Continue and changes the message's class. Clicking Continue sets the text to Accepted. Checking Show help displays the ng-show paragraph, hides the ng-hide paragraph and creates the ng-if block. Unchecking it removes the temporary note input completely; its unsaved DOM-local text is lost. By contrast, a hidden ng-show block remains in the DOM with its state/watchers.

Limitations / precautions — performance and security considerations

Use ng-if when avoiding an inactive subtree's nodes/watchers is valuable, and ng-show when preserving an often-toggled subtree is useful. This is a trade-off rather than a rule that one is always faster. Avoid overriding AngularJS's ng-hide styling unintentionally.

Hidden or disabled UI does not secure an API or hide data from a user inspecting the page. Never send confidential information merely because an element is hidden. Sanitize/validate any data used in URLs or style values according to its context.

Conclusion: DOM directives declaratively connect UI state to model conditions. The central exam distinction is between hiding an existing node, removing/recreating a node, and changing a control's property; they have different state, accessibility and performance consequences.

Long 51
Question
Explain ng-model, ng-init and ng-repeat directives of Angular JS with example. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:
