Introduction: AngularJS's ng-model, ng-init and ng-repeat connect editable data, initialization and repeated presentation. They belong to the AngularJS 1.x directive system and use expressions evaluated against a scope.

Purpose and syntax

Directive Syntax Role
ng-init ng-init="student={...}" Evaluate an initialization expression
ng-model ng-model="student.name" Bind an editable control to a model value
ng-repeat ng-repeat="course in courses track by course" Create one template instance per item

Detailed explanation

ng-init runs an initialization expression in the scope where the directive is linked. It can assign numbers, strings, objects or arrays. It is not a database load function or a replacement for controllers; move substantial initialization and business logic into proper application code.

ng-model handles synchronization between supported controls and the model, along with parser/formatter and validation behavior. Text inputs commonly provide strings, number inputs have numeric parsing, and a select connects a choice to a model value. Use object paths to keep ownership clear.

ng-repeat creates repeated DOM blocks and child scopes. Each instance exposes the current item and positional locals such as $index. A stable tracking expression helps AngularJS reuse the correct block when items change. The repeated collection itself is not copied into unrelated independent datasets.

Example: algorithm and complete example

Initialize one student and the allowed courses → bind name/course controls → generate options from the course array → display the current profile and a repeated course list. Save this HTML beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x library.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="selectionApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Student course selection</title></head>
<body ng-init="student={name:'Asha',course:'BCA'}; courses=['BCA','BBA','BSc']">
  <h1>Choose a course</h1>
  <label>Name <input ng-model="student.name"></label>
  <label>Course
    <select ng-model="student.course">
      <option ng-repeat="course in courses track by course" value="{{course}}">{{course}}</option>
    </select>
  </label>
  <p>{{student.name}} selected {{student.course}}.</p>
  <h2>Available courses</h2>
  <ul><li ng-repeat="course in courses track by course">{{$index + 1}}. {{course}}</li></ul>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>angular.module('selectionApp', []);</script>
</body></html>

Working and sample output

Initially, student.name is Asha and student.course is BCA, so the sentence is Asha selected BCA. ng-repeat generates three options and three list items from the same unique string array. Changing the name to Ravi and selecting BBA updates the sentence to Ravi selected BBA without reloading the document.

The option's value is explicitly the corresponding course string, matching the type held in the model. For complex object selections, AngularJS's ng-options often gives better identity/type handling than manually repeating options; this example deliberately uses ng-repeat because the question asks for it.

Limitations / precautions — edge cases

The tracking expression assumes course strings are unique. If duplicate codes are allowed, model them as records with unique IDs rather than using an unstable identity casually. An empty course list creates no repeated choices; real forms should handle that condition and validate selection. Recreating a scope can rerun its initialization, so ng-init should not contain irreversible operations.

Together, the directives demonstrate initialization, user-to-model interaction and collection-driven rendering. Their separation is important: ng-init creates starting values, ng-model keeps controls connected, and ng-repeat expands data into UI instances.

Conclusion: ng-model edits values, ng-init initializes a scope expression and ng-repeat renders a collection. The example links these roles without confusing model changes with repeated-template identity.

Long 52
Question
What are Angular JS directives? Write on ng-model and ng-repeat directives. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: AngularJS directives are markers recognized by the framework's HTML compiler to attach behavior and bindings to DOM elements. Examples include ng-app, ng-controller, ng-model and ng-repeat; applications can register custom directives through .directive(). They let templates describe interactions without manually updating every affected node.

Definition of directives

This answer focuses on ng-model and ng-repeat, which work well together for editable lists. The API is AngularJS 1.8.x, not modern Angular's [(ngModel)] and *ngFor syntax.

ng-model in detail

ng-model="expression" connects a control to an assignable scope expression. It supports text, checkbox, select and other input types through appropriate parsers/formatters. In a named form, the control also exposes validation state such as $error, $dirty and $touched. A model change updates the view, and a valid user edit updates the model.

For a checkbox, the model typically represents a Boolean; for a numeric input AngularJS parses numbers. Invalid input can make the model value undefined under normal settings, so calculations should not blindly assume every draft is valid. ng-model-options can configure update events/debouncing, but is not necessary for this basic example.

ng-repeat in detail

ng-repeat="item in items track by item.id" repeats a block with one child scope per item. It can expose index/first/last/even/odd locals and reflect additions, removals or reordering. Stable IDs preserve record identity; duplicate tracking keys are errors. Object-property paths such as item.qty also avoid the primitive shadowing pitfalls that can arise across nested scopes.

Example: complete editable-cart example

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="cartApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Editable cart</title></head>
<body ng-controller="CartController as vm">
  <h1>Shopping cart</h1>
  <ul>
    <li ng-repeat="item in vm.items track by item.id">
      <span>{{item.name}} — {{item.price | currency:'₹':2}}</span>
      <label>Quantity
        <input type="number" min="0" step="1" required ng-model="item.qty">
      </label>
    </li>
  </ul>
  <p>Total: {{vm.total() | currency:'₹':2}}</p>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('cartApp', []).controller('CartController', function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.items = [
        {id: 101, name: 'Notebook', price: 80, qty: 2},
        {id: 102, name: 'Pen', price: 20, qty: 3}
      ];
      vm.total = function() {
        return vm.items.reduce(function(sum, item) {
          var qty = typeof item.qty === 'number' && item.qty >= 0 ? item.qty : 0;
          return sum + item.price * qty;
        }, 0);
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Algorithm, input and output

Initialize two cart objects → repeat a row per object → bind each quantity input to that object's property → sum valid quantities times prices → format the total. The initial result is 2 × 80 + 3 × 20 = ₹220.00. Changing notebook quantity to 1 produces ₹140.00. Quantity zero contributes nothing.

The total function is pure and small; it may run repeatedly during digest checks. Invalid/cleared quantities contribute zero in this demonstration to avoid a NaN display, but a checkout workflow should also explicitly show field errors and block submission until valid.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

Do not use repeated rows to trust a client-provided price: a server must verify prices, availability and quantities before accepting an order. Large lists can create substantial DOM/watch overhead. Stable item IDs and object-based models make the binding predictable. ng-model handles each editable value, while ng-repeat handles how many editable views exist and which record each belongs to.

Conclusion: ng-model supplies editable binding and control state, while ng-repeat creates tracked instances for collection items. Together they support an editable cart with predictable updates and identity.

Long 53
Question
Explain Component Communication using @Input() and @Output() with an example. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: In modern Angular, @Input() exposes a child component property for parent-to-child data binding. @Output() exposes an event, commonly represented by EventEmitter<T>, that the child emits to notify its parent. This keeps ownership clear: the parent owns shared state, while the child displays it and requests changes.

Parent–child communication

The output is a notification with a typed payload, not direct mutation of the parent's field. Angular output events are not ordinary DOM events that automatically bubble through unrelated ancestors.

Syntax and responsibilities

  • @Input() count = 0; declares an input with a default.
  • <counter-child [count]="count"> binds a parent expression to it.
  • @Output() countChange = new EventEmitter<number>(); declares an event.
  • countChange.emit(next) sends the payload.
  • (countChange)="count = $event" handles it in the parent template.

The decorators remain valid for this syllabus; newer Angular also offers function-based input/output APIs. Do not mix this mechanism with AngularJS's $scope events or React props syntax.

Example: complete standalone example

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project with standard polyfills and <app-root> in index.html. This is a complete educational src/main.ts.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component, EventEmitter, Input, Output} from '@angular/core';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';

@Component({
  selector: 'counter-child', standalone: true,
  template: `<h2>Child counter</h2><p>Count: {{count}}</p>
    <button type="button" (click)="increment()">Add one</button>`
})
class CounterChild {
  @Input() count = 0;
  @Output() countChange = new EventEmitter<number>();
  increment() { this.countChange.emit(this.count + 1); }
}
@Component({
  selector: 'app-root', standalone: true, imports: [CounterChild],
  template: `<h1>Parent</h1><p>Parent value: {{count}}</p>
    <counter-child [count]="count" (countChange)="setCount($event)"></counter-child>
    <button type="button" (click)="count = 0">Reset from parent</button>`
})
class AppComponent {
  count = 0;
  setCount(next: number) { this.count = next; }
}
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Algorithm and sample output

Initialize parent count → bind it into the child → on a child click emit current count plus one → parent handles the payload and updates its count → binding delivers the new value to the child. Initially both displays are 0. Two child clicks change both to 2. Clicking the parent's Reset changes both back to 0.

The child does not perform this.count++ and hope the parent notices. It emits the proposed next value, leaving the owner responsible for accepting or modifying that request. This pattern also supports validation or limits in the parent handler.

Limitations / precautions — two-way shorthand and precautions

When an input is named count and the corresponding output is named countChange, <counter-child [(count)]="count"> is shorthand for the two explicit bindings. The underlying flow still consists of a value and a change event; it is not shared mutable memory.

An input can receive an object reference. Mutating its nested properties in the child can unexpectedly affect the parent and complicate change detection, so prefer immutable updates and change notifications. EventEmitter is intended for component outputs; application-wide communication usually belongs in an appropriately designed service rather than a chain of unrelated outputs.

Conclusion: Inputs carry data down and outputs report events up. Explicit property/event contracts make components reusable and testable while preserving a clear owner for state.

Long 54
Question
Differentiate between Structural and Attribute Directives with examples. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: In classic modern Angular syntax, a structural directive creates, removes or repeats embedded views, changing DOM structure. An attribute directive changes the behavior or appearance of an existing host element without primarily controlling an embedded view's existence. Examples here target Angular 17, where the syllabus's *ngIf and *ngFor syntax is supported. Newer control-flow blocks such as @if are a separate syntax.

Comparison

Basis Structural directive Attribute directive
Main task Add/remove/repeat a view Modify an existing host's behavior/style
Common classic notation *ngIf, *ngFor [ngClass], [ngStyle], custom attribute
Typical infrastructure TemplateRef and ViewContainerRef Host bindings/listeners or element integration
DOM effect Number/presence of nodes can change Host remains, with changed properties/classes
Example use Conditional panel, repeated row Highlighting, validation styling
Important limit One structural shorthand per host element Multiple attributes can usually coexist

The asterisk is template shorthand. For example, a block using *ngIf="visible" can be understood as an <ng-template [ngIf]="visible"> containing that block. Use <ng-container> or nested templates when two structural operations are needed; do not put *ngIf and *ngFor on the same element.

Example: complete example

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project with <app-root> and standard polyfills. This main.ts includes a small custom attribute directive.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component, Directive, HostBinding, Input} from '@angular/core';
import {CommonModule} from '@angular/common';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';

@Directive({selector: '[appHighlight]', standalone: true})
class HighlightDirective {
  @Input() appHighlight = '#fff3c4';
  @HostBinding('style.backgroundColor')
  get backgroundColor(): string { return this.appHighlight; }
}
@Component({
  selector: 'app-root', standalone: true,
  imports: [CommonModule, HighlightDirective],
  styles: ['.strong {font-weight: bold;}'],
  template: `<h1>Directives</h1>
    <button (click)="visible = !visible">Toggle list</button>
    <ng-container *ngIf="visible">
      <ul><li *ngFor="let course of courses"
        [ngClass]="{strong: course === 'React'}" appHighlight="#edf7f1">
        {{course}}
      </li></ul>
    </ng-container>`
})
class AppComponent { visible = true; courses = ['React', 'MongoDB']; }
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Algorithm, working and output

Bootstrap the component → if visible, create the list container's embedded view → repeat one list item per course → apply conditional classes and the custom background binding. Initially two items appear on a pale background, with React bold. Toggling visibility removes the list's view; toggling again recreates it.

ng-container does not add a normal wrapper element to the DOM, making it useful for structural grouping. The custom directive's selector matches appHighlight; its input supplies a color and its host binding updates the element's background. It does not create or remove list items, so it is an attribute directive.

Limitations / precautions — important nuances

Not every directive name beginning with ng is structural, and not every behavioral change requires *. ngSwitch, for example, is placed on a host while its case/default directives control embedded views. A component is a special directive with a template, not merely a synonym for all attribute directives.

Structural removal destroys the associated view state; CSS hiding preserves the node. Use the right mechanism for the desired lifecycle behavior, import required standalone directives or CommonModule, and avoid direct unsafe DOM HTML injection. The key distinction is view structure versus host behavior/appearance.

Conclusion: Structural directives create or remove views; attribute directives modify an existing element's behavior or appearance. Correct syntax and awareness of view creation distinguish the two categories.

Long 55
Question
Explain *ngIf, ngFor, and ngSwitch directives with examples. …
LongUnit 44.2 Angular directives & component communication
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: The question refers to classic modern Angular control-flow directives: *ngIf, *ngFor and ngSwitch with *ngSwitchCase/*ngSwitchDefault. The ngFor shorthand normally includes *; the ngSwitch host itself does not. These examples target Angular 17. Newer Angular supports @if, @for and @switch; the historical syntax is retained here to match the syllabus.

Ambiguity note: The question omits the asterisk on ngFor and abbreviates switch syntax. Classic Angular uses *ngFor, [ngSwitch], *ngSwitchCase and *ngSwitchDefault; the source wording is retained.

1. *ngIf

*ngIf="condition; else alternative" creates a view when the expression is truthy and can render another template when false. It removes/recreates the view rather than just setting display: none, so local DOM state and child lifecycles are affected.

2. *ngFor

*ngFor="let item of items; index as i; trackBy: trackItem" repeats a view for an iterable. Positional locals help display row numbers; a stable trackBy return value improves identity preservation when object instances are replaced. Do not confuse item identity with its current index in a reorderable list.

3. ngSwitch

[ngSwitch]="value" selects case views. Each *ngSwitchCase compares a case expression, while *ngSwitchDefault handles no match. Unlike JavaScript's switch, templates do not require break statements. Keep case types consistent with the model values.

Example: complete main.ts

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project with standard polyfills and an index page containing <app-root>.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component} from '@angular/core';
import {CommonModule} from '@angular/common';
import {FormsModule} from '@angular/forms';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';

type Student = {id: number; name: string};
@Component({
  selector: 'app-root', standalone: true, imports: [CommonModule, FormsModule],
  template: `<h1>Admission dashboard</h1>
    <button (click)="open = !open">Toggle admission</button>
    <p *ngIf="open; else closed">Admission is open.</p>
    <ng-template #closed><p>Admission is closed.</p></ng-template>
    <ul><li *ngFor="let student of students; index as i; trackBy: trackStudent">
      {{i + 1}}. {{student.name}}
    </li></ul>
    <p *ngIf="students.length === 0">No students.</p>
    <label>Course <select [(ngModel)]="course">
      <option value="BCA">BCA</option><option value="BBA">BBA</option>
      <option value="OTHER">Other</option>
    </select></label>
    <section [ngSwitch]="course">
      <p *ngSwitchCase="'BCA'">Computer applications programme</p>
      <p *ngSwitchCase="'BBA'">Business administration programme</p>
      <p *ngSwitchDefault>Select a supported programme.</p>
    </section>`
})
class AppComponent {
  open = true;
  course = 'BCA';
  students: Student[] = [{id: 1, name: 'Asha'}, {id: 2, name: 'Ravi'}];
  trackStudent(index: number, student: Student): number { return student.id; }
}
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Working and expected output

Algorithm: evaluate admission flag → create the matching message → repeat the students → bind the selected course → show the corresponding case. Initially the page displays Admission is open, students 1. Asha and 2. Ravi, and the computer applications message. Toggling admission displays the closed template. Selecting BBA displays the business administration message; Other displays the default.

CommonModule makes the classic directives available, while FormsModule supplies ngModel. The select is outside a form, so no form registration name is required here. A list inside a form would introduce separate naming considerations for its controls.

Limitations / precautions — edge cases

An empty student array produces the explicit empty-state paragraph. Stable IDs must remain unique; duplicate tracking IDs can cause incorrect rendering or diagnostics. Only one structural shorthand is allowed on an element; use ng-container when combining conditions and repetition. These directives express conditional, repeated and multi-case views without manual DOM insertion/removal.

Conclusion: Classic ngIf, ngFor and ngSwitch express conditional inclusion, repetition and case selection. Their microsyntax, containers and imports must match the stated Angular version.

4.3 Angular data binding

Long 56
Question
Write an Angular JS code to display FirstName and LastName entered by the user into their respective textboxes and display output in the following form: First name: Robert, Last name: Desoza, Hello Robert Desoza. …
LongUnit 44.3 Angular data binding
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Create an AngularJS interface with separate FirstName and LastName textboxes and display the values in the exact requested form: First name: Robert, Last name: Desoza, Hello Robert Desoza for the sample input. This is a live-binding exercise, so no submit button or backend is necessary.

Aim and binding approach

Use ng-model for the two editable controls and interpolation for the output. A controller owns the fields through a vm alias; a derived full-name function avoids maintaining a second, potentially inconsistent copy of the same information.

Algorithm

  1. Create an AngularJS module and controller.
  2. Initialize the two name strings to empty values.
  3. Bind each textbox to its corresponding property.
  4. Display each individual field under its required label.
  5. When both fields contain text, concatenate them with one separating space for the greeting.

Example: complete HTML program

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="nameApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>First and last name</title></head>
<body ng-controller="NameController as vm">
  <h1>Name binding</h1>
  <label>FirstName <input name="firstName" type="text"
    autocomplete="given-name" ng-model="vm.firstName"></label>
  <label>LastName <input name="lastName" type="text"
    autocomplete="family-name" ng-model="vm.lastName"></label>
  <section aria-live="polite">
    <p>First name: {{vm.firstName}}</p>
    <p>Last name: {{vm.lastName}}</p>
    <p ng-if="vm.firstName && vm.lastName">Hello {{vm.fullName()}}</p>
  </section>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('nameApp', []).controller('NameController', function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.firstName = '';
      vm.lastName = '';
      vm.fullName = function() {
        return [vm.firstName, vm.lastName].filter(Boolean).join(' ');
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Explanation of important lines

ng-app="nameApp" matches the created module. ng-controller="NameController as vm" exposes an explicit object that owns the model properties. Each ng-model path is distinct, so typing a last name cannot overwrite the first name.

Interpolation reads the current model after AngularJS processes a view edit. The full-name function is pure and performs a very small calculation; it does not mutate data or make a request during digest checking. ng-if avoids showing an incomplete greeting while a required name part is still empty. The individually labelled lines remain visible to show the current entries.

Sample input and expected output

Enter Robert in FirstName and Desoza in LastName. The output is:

Expected output
First name: Robert
Last name: Desoza
Hello Robert Desoza

Changing Robert to Asha immediately produces First name: Asha and Hello Asha Desoza. Clearing either field removes the complete greeting until both are populated; it does not show an undefined value.

Limitations / precautions — edge cases, safety

Text interpolation writes text, not executable HTML. Do not replace it with untrusted template compilation or raw HTML insertion. Names may contain spaces, apostrophes or non-Latin characters, so this example does not impose an artificial alphabet-only rule.

The local framework file is needed only to run this separate example. The question bank itself works offline without AngularJS. The solution demonstrates two-way control binding and one-way textual display, giving the exact sample wording while keeping the model simple and avoiding redundant state.

Conclusion: Two model-bound textboxes supply the first and last names, and expressions display both separate labels and the combined greeting. The values remain user-editable rather than hardcoded output.

Long 57
Question
Write a code to create 2 radio buttons (show and hide) and a paragraph tag using AngularJS; clicking Show displays the paragraph and clicking Hide hides it. …
LongUnit 44.3 Angular data binding
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Create exactly two radio choices, show and hide, controlling the visibility of a paragraph with AngularJS. The important detail is to bind Boolean values with ng-value, not the strings "true" and "false": both nonempty strings would be truthy in a visibility expression.

Aim and key concept

Use one shared model property for both radios and the same native name so they form a mutually exclusive group. ng-show displays the paragraph when that property is true and hides it when false.

Algorithm

Initialize showParagraph to false → bind both radio buttons to it → assign true through the show radio and false through the hide radio → evaluate the paragraph's ng-show expression after each change. No manual click listener or DOM query is required.

Example: complete program

Save this HTML beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="visibilityApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Radio visibility control</title></head>
<body ng-controller="VisibilityController as vm">
  <h1>Paragraph visibility</h1>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Choose paragraph visibility</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="visibility"
      ng-model="vm.showParagraph" ng-value="true">show</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="visibility"
      ng-model="vm.showParagraph" ng-value="false">hide</label>
  </fieldset>
  <p ng-show="vm.showParagraph">This paragraph is controlled by the radio buttons.</p>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('visibilityApp', [])
      .controller('VisibilityController', function() {
        this.showParagraph = false;
      });
  </script>
</body></html>

Explanation and expected behavior

ng-model links both radios to the same property. ng-value="true" is evaluated as a Boolean expression, and ng-value="false" as the opposite Boolean. The initial false value selects hide and keeps the paragraph hidden.

Action Model value Paragraph
Initial load false Hidden
Select show true Visible
Select hide false Hidden again
Select the already selected option Unchanged Remains in current state

The browser handles keyboard navigation within the radio group; associated labels enlarge the clickable target. The fieldset/legend communicates that the two options are one choice.

ng-show versus alternatives

ng-show toggles the AngularJS ng-hide CSS class and retains the paragraph node in the DOM. This differs from ng-if, which creates/removes its block and scope. ng-hide="!vm.showParagraph" could express equivalent visible behavior, but ng-show directly matches the property name and is clearer here.

Do not write ng-show="{{vm.showParagraph}}"; directive attributes take expressions directly. Do not use two separate model properties, because that would break the intended single state. Also avoid assigning a string value="false" and then treating it as a Boolean condition.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

Hidden content is still delivered to the browser and can be inspected, so visibility is not access control. If confidential content must be protected, authorization must happen before delivery. This program fulfills the requested show/hide interaction using Boolean radio binding and declarative visibility, without unnecessary event handlers or direct DOM manipulation.

Conclusion: Two radio buttons select one Boolean value, and ng-show derives paragraph visibility from it. Boolean binding avoids the common mistake of treating the nonempty string 'false' as false.

4.3.2–4.4 Expressions, filters & pipes

Long 58
Question
⭐⭐⭐⭐ Explain expressions and filters in AngularJS. …
LongUnit 44.3.2–4.4 Expressions, filters & pipes★ × 4
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: An AngularJS expression evaluates data from the current scope for use in a template. Interpolation normally surrounds it with double braces, such as {{student.name}}; directives use the expression directly, such as ng-bind="student.name".

AngularJS expressions

Expressions support property access, arithmetic, string combinations, arrays/objects and function calls. They are not full JavaScript programs: general declarations and control-flow statements such as for and if are not inserted as template expressions. They do not directly expose ordinary browser globals such as window. Tolerant handling of some missing values is a convenience, not a security sandbox; never compile untrusted text into templates.

Example Meaning
{{2 + 3}} Arithmetic result 5
{{student.first + ' ' + student.last}} Concatenated names
{{items[0].name}} Property of an array element
ng-bind="total()" Text from a scope/controller function

Keep expressions small and side-effect-free because the digest process can evaluate them repeatedly.

Filters and syntax

A filter transforms a value for display or produces a transformed collection. Template syntax is expression | filterName:argument1:argument2; several filters can be chained. The pipe symbol here is AngularJS filter syntax, not JavaScript's bitwise operator.

Examples include uppercase/lowercase text, number/currency/date formatting, filter for array selection, orderBy for array ordering and limitTo for limiting values. Built-in presentation filters do not ordinarily change the original model. In JavaScript code, inject $filter and call the requested named filter.

Example: complete example

Save beside local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="expressionApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Expressions and filters</title></head>
<body ng-controller="ExampleController as vm">
  <h1>{{vm.title | uppercase}}</h1>
  <p>Arithmetic: {{2 + 3}}</p>
  <p>Total: {{vm.quantity * vm.price | currency:'₹':2}}</p>
  <p>Date: {{vm.day | date:'dd/MM/yyyy'}}</p>
  <label>Search name <input ng-model="vm.query"></label>
  <ul>
    <li ng-repeat="student in vm.students | filter:{name:vm.query} | orderBy:'-marks' | limitTo:2 track by student.id">
      {{student.name}} — {{student.marks | number:1}}
    </li>
  </ul>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('expressionApp', []).controller('ExampleController', function() {
      this.title = 'Student results';
      this.quantity = 3;
      this.price = 50;
      this.day = new Date(2026, 0, 15);
      this.query = '';
      this.students = [
        {id: 1, name: 'Asha', marks: 80},
        {id: 2, name: 'Ravi', marks: 92},
        {id: 3, name: 'Mira', marks: 70}
      ];
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Algorithm and expected output

Initialize controller data → evaluate expressions → pass their values through formatting filters → filter/sort/limit the student array → render the selected rows. With the standard en-US locale, initial output includes STUDENT RESULTS, Arithmetic: 5, Total: ₹150.00, Date: 15/01/2026, then Ravi — 92.0 and Asha — 80.0.

The filter order matters: search occurs before descending ordering and limiting. Typing Mira selects that student first, so she appears even though she was not originally in the unfiltered top two. track by student.id follows the complete filter chain and gives stable DOM identity.

Limitations / precautions — caveats

Currency/date output depends on locale and date/timezone interpretation; filters do not convert currency units or change database values. limitTo truncates a list, not the stored collection. Large sorting/filtering operations repeated during digest checks can be expensive; precompute or paginate when appropriate.

Modern Angular calls similar display transformations pipes and does not ship AngularJS's filter/orderBy as equivalent built-ins. An exam answer should distinguish the AngularJS expression language, display filters and model-changing application logic rather than mixing their syntax.

Conclusion: AngularJS expressions derive template values and filters transform their presentation. Small, pure expressions and explicit filter parameters keep the displayed result understandable and safe.

Long 59
Question
Explain Filters and Controller of AngularJS in detail. …
LongUnit 44.3.2–4.4 Expressions, filters & pipes
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: An AngularJS controller prepares data and actions for a view; a filter transforms an input for presentation or selection. Controllers are registered with .controller(), filters with .filter(), and both belong to an AngularJS module. Reusable data access/business logic should normally be placed in services rather than crowded into controllers or templates.

Filters and controllers: different roles

A controller can expose data through $scope or through an instance alias such as ProfileController as vm. A filter factory returns a transformation function. Prefer pure transformations: do not make network requests, change model state or emit side effects during filter evaluation.

Example: built-in filters and programmatic use

Filter Example purpose
uppercase / lowercase Text casing
currency / number Locale-aware numeric display
date Date/time formatting
filter Select array items matching a condition
orderBy / limitTo Sort and limit a display collection
json Debug-oriented JSON text

Template syntax is value | filterName:argument. To use a filter from JavaScript, inject the $filter service and call $filter('uppercase')('bca'). The service returns the named filter function; it is not itself the controller.

Complete example with a custom filter

Save the following beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="profileFilterApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Controller and filters</title></head>
<body ng-controller="ProfileController as vm">
  <h1>Student profile</h1>
  <label>Full name <input ng-model="vm.name"></label>
  <p>Name: {{vm.name | uppercase}}</p>
  <p>Initials: {{vm.name | initials}}</p>
  <p>Course: {{vm.courseLabel}}</p>
  <p>Fee: {{vm.fee | currency:'₹':2}}</p>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('profileFilterApp', [])
      .filter('initials', function() {
        return function(value) {
          if (value === null || value === undefined) return '';
          return String(value).trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean)
            .map(function(part) { return part.charAt(0).toUpperCase(); }).join('');
        };
      })
      .controller('ProfileController', ['$filter', function($filter) {
        this.name = 'Asha Patel';
        this.fee = 1250;
        this.courseLabel = $filter('uppercase')('bca');
      }]);
  </script>
</body></html>

Algorithm and working

Create the module → register a transformation returning initials → construct the controller with its injected filter service → initialize profile data → render the data through template filters → update the name through ng-model and recompute displayed transformations.

Initial output: Name: ASHA PATEL; Initials: AP; Course: BCA; Fee: ₹1,250.00 with the standard en-US locale. Replacing the input with Robert Desoza changes initials to RD and uppercase display to ROBERT DESOZA. The original editable string retains its normal casing because the filters transform output, not vm.name itself.

Limitations / precautions — explanation and edge cases

The custom filter accepts null/undefined and returns an empty string instead of throwing. Trimming and splitting on whitespace avoids empty initials from repeated spaces. This is a simple initial-letter policy, not a universal rule for every culture's personal names. Filter registration occurs on the module before the template uses it; a misspelled filter name causes a lookup error.

Array-style $filter annotation remains safe under minification. Controller construction happens for each controller instance, whereas the registered filter function should be reusable and stateless for ordinary input/output transformations.

Conclusion: Controllers provide model/action context; filters provide focused presentation transformations. Keeping these responsibilities distinct makes code easier to test, prevents accidental mutation during rendering and avoids burying business operations in repeated template evaluations.

Long 60
Question
⭐ Explain AngularJS filters with suitable examples. …
LongUnit 44.3.2–4.4 Expressions, filters & pipes★ × 1
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: An AngularJS filter transforms an expression's output or returns a selected/ordered subset for display. The general syntax is {{ value | filterName:arg1:arg2 }}. Filters may be chained from left to right, and the original model is not normally changed by built-in presentation filters.

Definition and syntax

In a controller/service, inject $filter and call a named filter as a function. AngularJS filters are part of the 1.x API; modern Angular has pipes and does not provide identical built-in array-filtering APIs.

Example: important built-in filters with examples

Filter Example template expression Result / purpose
uppercase {{'React' \| uppercase}} REACT
lowercase {{'ANGULAR' \| lowercase}} angular
currency {{1234.5 \| currency:'₹':2}} ₹1,234.50 under en-US locale
number {{1234.567 \| number:2}} 1,234.57 under en-US locale
date {{day \| date:'dd/MM/yyyy'}} Formatted date, e.g. 15/01/2026
json {{record \| json}} JSON text useful for debugging
limitTo {{'AngularJS' \| limitTo:7}} Angular
filter items \| filter:{name:query} Matching array entries
orderBy items \| orderBy:'-marks' Highest marks first

currency changes display, not currency value: ₹ and $ are not exchanged by supplying a new symbol. The date format uses uppercase/lowercase pattern letters with different meanings, so copy the intended pattern carefully.

Complete example

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="filterDemo">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>AngularJS filters</title></head>
<body ng-controller="FilterController as vm">
  <h1>{{vm.heading | uppercase}}</h1>
  <p>Amount: {{vm.amount | currency:'₹':2}}</p>
  <p>Decimal: {{vm.amount | number:1}}</p>
  <p>Date: {{vm.day | date:'dd/MM/yyyy'}}</p>
  <label>Search <input ng-model="vm.search"></label>
  <ol>
    <li ng-repeat="s in vm.students | filter:{name:vm.search} | orderBy:'-marks' | limitTo:2 track by s.id">
      {{s.name | uppercase}}: {{s.marks}}
    </li>
  </ol>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('filterDemo', []).controller('FilterController', function() {
      this.heading = 'Results'; this.amount = 1234.5;
      this.day = new Date(2026, 0, 15); this.search = '';
      this.students = [
        {id: 1, name: 'Asha', marks: 80},
        {id: 2, name: 'Ravi', marks: 90},
        {id: 3, name: 'Mira', marks: 75}
      ];
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Working and expected results

Algorithm: initialize data → format scalar values → filter the list by search → sort the matches → retain two records → render their names and marks. Initially the heading is RESULTS, the amount is ₹1,234.50, the decimal display is 1,234.5, and the date is 15/01/2026. The first two records are RAVI: 90 and ASHA: 80.

Typing Mira produces only MIRA: 75 because selection happens before the limit. The underlying array still has all three records in its original order. Clearing the query restores the unfiltered top two.

Limitations / precautions — custom filters, performance

Custom filters are registered with .filter('name', function() { return function(input) { ... }; }). Their transformations should be deterministic and avoid modifying their input. Expensive sorting/filtering over large collections during digest checks can harm responsiveness; precompute, paginate or filter on the server where appropriate.

Locale affects grouping, decimal separators, currency symbols and date presentation. Do not use json to display objects containing passwords or other secrets. Filters are for readable/selected output; they should not become a hidden place for state-changing business operations.

Conclusion: AngularJS filters format or select view data without inherently rewriting the model. Their order, parameters, locale and runtime cost must be considered when composing a display pipeline.

Long 61
Question
Explain Angular built-in pipes in detail. …
LongUnit 44.3.2–4.4 Expressions, filters & pipes
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: A pipe is a modern Angular template transformation: {{ value | pipeName:argument }}. Pipes format values without requiring repetitive formatting code in each component. This answer uses Angular 17-style standalone components and CommonModule, which supplies the built-in pipes used below. Standalone pipes can also be imported individually.

Ambiguity note: “Pipes” is interpreted as modern Angular terminology. AngularJS has filters with a similar presentation role but a different registration/import system.

Definition and version

Do not confuse these pipes with AngularJS's filter registry. Modern Angular does not provide AngularJS's general filter or orderBy pipes as built-ins; select/sort arrays in well-designed component/service logic or an appropriate custom pipe.

Main built-in pipes

Template name / class Purpose Example result
uppercase / UpperCasePipe Uppercase text React → REACT
lowercase / LowerCasePipe Lowercase text WEB → web
titlecase / TitleCasePipe Capitalize words web design → Web Design
number / DecimalPipe Digit/grouping formatting 1234.5 → 1,234.50 with 1.2-2
percent / PercentPipe Ratio as percentage 0.85 → 85%
currency / CurrencyPipe Currency-aware display 1234.5 with INR → ₹1,234.50 in en-US
date / DatePipe Date/time formatting A date → 15/01/2026
slice / SlicePipe Subset of string/array Index interval, end exclusive
json / JsonPipe JSON display for debugging Object as formatted JSON text
async / AsyncPipe Latest Promise/Observable value Updates view; handles subscription lifecycle
keyvalue / KeyValuePipe Object/Map entries for iteration Key/value pair array
i18nPlural, i18nSelect Choose localized message alternatives Quantity/category-specific text

Parameters, locale and purity

The digit pattern minIntegerDigits.minFractionDigits-maxFractionDigits, such as 1.2-2, requests at least one integer digit and exactly two fractional digits. Locale controls separators and symbol placement; en-US data is normally available by default, while other locales may need registration/configuration.

Most formatting pipes are pure: Angular re-evaluates them when their primitive input value or object reference changes, not after every hidden nested mutation. Use immutable replacements when necessary. Not all pipes are pure; async, for example, manages an ongoing asynchronous source. Avoid assuming a pipe is merely a string formatter with no lifecycle implications.

Example: complete example

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project with standard polyfills and <app-root> in index.html.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component} from '@angular/core';
import {CommonModule} from '@angular/common';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';
import {of} from 'rxjs';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root', standalone: true, imports: [CommonModule],
  template: `<h1>{{title | titlecase}}</h1>
    <p>{{title | uppercase}}</p>
    <p>Amount: {{amount | number:'1.2-2':'en-US'}}</p>
    <p>INR: {{amount | currency:'INR':'symbol':'1.2-2':'en-US'}}</p>
    <p>Score: {{ratio | percent:'1.0-0':'en-US'}}</p>
    <p>Date: {{day | date:'dd/MM/yyyy':'UTC'}}</p>
    <p>Slice: {{letters | slice:1:3 | json}}</p>
    <p>Status: {{status$ | async}}</p>
    <ul><li *ngFor="let entry of profile | keyvalue">
      {{entry.key}}: {{entry.value}}
    </li></ul>`
})
class AppComponent {
  title = 'advanced web designing';
  amount = 1234.5; ratio = 0.85;
  day = new Date('2026-01-15T12:00:00Z');
  letters = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'];
  status$ = of('Ready');
  profile = {course: 'BCA', name: 'Asha'};
}
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Working and output

The page displays Advanced Web Designing, its uppercase version, 1,234.50, ₹1,234.50, 85%, and 15/01/2026. The slice contains B and C because index 1 is included and index 3 is excluded. async unwraps the Observable's Ready value; it also handles cleanup when a source is replaced or the view is destroyed.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

Currency formatting does not convert exchange rates. Date formatting must account for timezone; the example explicitly uses UTC. Do not display secrets through json. Pipes keep presentation transformations readable and composable, while state changes, authorization and expensive data processing should remain in appropriate application layers.

Conclusion: Angular pipes make template transformations readable and reusable. Import the required APIs and distinguish formatting from currency conversion, mutation or backend processing.

4.5 Angular forms & validation

Long 62
Question
⭐⭐ Explain Form and Form validation in Angular JS. Write suitable code. …
LongUnit 44.5 Angular forms & validation★ × 2
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: An AngularJS form groups named controls and tracks their values and validation state. ng-model connects each control to the model and supplies parsing, formatting and validation support. A named form, such as name="studentForm", exposes a form controller; named controls are available through it, for example studentForm.email.

Forms and validation in AngularJS

Validation checks input against rules such as required values, email format, length, range or a regular-expression pattern. It improves user feedback but cannot enforce backend security by itself. This answer uses AngularJS 1.8.x, not modern Angular's FormGroup/NgForm APIs.

Important states and validators

State / rule Meaning
$valid, $invalid Validation success/failure
$pristine, $dirty No view edit yet / edited or marked dirty
$untouched, $touched Not blurred yet / control has lost focus
$submitted Form has been submitted
$error Map of failed validator names
$pending Asynchronous validation is pending, if present
required Nonempty required value
type="email" Email-format validator
ng-minlength, ng-maxlength Length limits
ng-pattern, min, max Pattern or numeric-range rules

$invalid and $dirty are properties, not directives. A field may be dirty and valid, or touched and still pristine. Returning to its original value does not automatically make it pristine again.

Example: algorithm and complete example

Initialize model → bind named controls → show errors only after touch/submission → on submit, reject invalid/pending form state → copy a valid snapshot for display. Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="validationApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>AngularJS form validation</title></head>
<body ng-controller="FormController as vm">
  <h1>Student form</h1>
  <form name="studentForm" ng-submit="vm.submit(studentForm)" novalidate>
    <label>Name <input name="studentName" ng-model="vm.student.name"
      required ng-minlength="2" autocomplete="name"></label>
    <p ng-show="(studentForm.studentName.$touched || studentForm.$submitted) && studentForm.studentName.$invalid">
      Enter a name of at least two characters.
    </p>
    <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" ng-model="vm.student.email"
      required autocomplete="email"></label>
    <p ng-show="(studentForm.email.$touched || studentForm.$submitted) && studentForm.email.$error.required">Email is required.</p>
    <p ng-show="(studentForm.email.$touched || studentForm.$submitted) && studentForm.email.$error.email">Enter a valid email format.</p>
    <button type="submit">Validate</button>
  </form>
  <p role="alert" ng-bind="vm.message"></p>
  <section ng-if="vm.result"><h2>Validated details</h2>
    <p>{{vm.result.name}} — {{vm.result.email}}</p>
    <p>Local demonstration; nothing was saved to a server.</p>
  </section>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('validationApp', []).controller('FormController', function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.student = {name: '', email: ''}; vm.result = null; vm.message = '';
      vm.submit = function(form) {
        vm.result = null;
        if (form.$invalid || form.$pending) {
          vm.message = 'Please correct the highlighted fields.'; return;
        }
        vm.message = '';
        vm.result = angular.copy(vm.student);
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Working, sample input and output

novalidate disables the browser's native submission validation bubbles so AngularJS feedback controls the interaction; it does not disable AngularJS validators. ng-submit invokes the handler and, without an action URL, AngularJS prevents normal form navigation. Clicking Validate with empty fields reveals the errors through $submitted, even if nothing was touched yet.

Entering Asha Patel and [email protected] produces a validated detail summary. An email such as not-an-email triggers the email validator. angular.copy creates a snapshot, so subsequent draft edits do not silently modify the old result.

Limitations / precautions — security, edge cases

An invalid input may not be written to the model under normal AngularJS settings, so inspect form state rather than assuming the draft model contains every typed character. Pending asynchronous checks must also be handled before accepting a form. Repeat validation, identity checks and authorization on the server; never use a disabled button or $valid as a security boundary. Effective form validation combines named controls, explicit rules, well-timed feedback and a guarded submission handler.

Conclusion: AngularJS form validation combines named controls, rules, interaction states and a guarded submit handler. Helpful client feedback complements, but never replaces, server-side validation and authorization.

Long 63
Question
⭐ Create a student registration form using Angular JS and provide validations on the form fields. …
LongUnit 44.5 Angular forms & validation★ × 1
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Create an AngularJS student registration form with validation. Since fields are not prescribed, this example uses Roll No., Name, Email and Course. Roll numbers are digit strings so leading zeros are preserved; the allowed illustrative courses are BCA, BBA and BSc. All fields are required, and the name must contain at least two characters.

Aim and stated fields

This is a local registration-data demonstration, not a database-backed registration service. Use a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js beside the HTML file.

Algorithm

Initialize a student object → bind named controls → apply required/pattern/length/email rules → show errors after touch or attempted submit → reject invalid/pending state and disallowed course values → copy the valid student into a display snapshot.

Example: complete program

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="studentRegistrationApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Student registration</title></head>
<body ng-controller="RegistrationController as vm">
  <h1>Student registration</h1>
  <form name="reg" ng-submit="vm.submit(reg)" novalidate>
    <label>Roll No. <input name="rollno" type="text" inputmode="numeric"
      ng-model="vm.student.rollno" ng-pattern="/^[0-9]+$/" required></label>
    <p ng-show="(reg.rollno.$touched || reg.$submitted) && reg.rollno.$invalid">Enter a digit-only roll number.</p>
    <label>Name <input name="fullName" ng-model="vm.student.name"
      ng-minlength="2" required autocomplete="name"></label>
    <p ng-show="(reg.fullName.$touched || reg.$submitted) && reg.fullName.$invalid">Name must contain at least two characters.</p>
    <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" ng-model="vm.student.email"
      required autocomplete="email"></label>
    <p ng-show="(reg.email.$touched || reg.$submitted) && reg.email.$invalid">A valid email is required.</p>
    <label>Course <select name="course" ng-model="vm.student.course" required>
      <option value="">Choose a course</option><option value="BCA">BCA</option>
      <option value="BBA">BBA</option><option value="BSc">BSc</option>
    </select></label>
    <p ng-show="(reg.course.$touched || reg.$submitted) && reg.course.$invalid">Choose a course.</p>
    <button type="submit">Validate registration</button>
  </form>
  <p role="alert" ng-bind="vm.error"></p>
  <section ng-if="vm.result"><h2>Validated student</h2>
    <p>Roll No.: {{vm.result.rollno}}</p><p>Name: {{vm.result.name}}</p>
    <p>Email: {{vm.result.email}}</p><p>Course: {{vm.result.course}}</p>
    <p>Demonstration only; no record was saved.</p>
  </section>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('studentRegistrationApp', []).controller('RegistrationController', function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.student = {rollno: '', name: '', email: '', course: ''};
      vm.result = null; vm.error = '';
      vm.submit = function(form) {
        vm.result = null;
        if (form.$invalid || form.$pending || ['BCA', 'BBA', 'BSc'].indexOf(vm.student.course) < 0) {
          vm.error = 'Correct all fields before continuing.'; return;
        }
        vm.error = '';
        vm.result = angular.copy(vm.student);
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Explanation and sample result

The form name exposes reg, and each control name exposes validation state below it. ng-pattern checks the full roll-number string; inputmode is a keyboard hint, not validation. Text ng-model trimming prevents a whitespace-only name from satisfying required validation. The course allowlist in the handler demonstrates that visible select options are not the only check.

Sample input: roll 007, name Asha Patel, email [email protected], course BCA. Output: those four values appear under Validated student, with roll 007 unchanged. The copied result remains a snapshot while the draft is edited.

Limitations / precautions — tests, limitations

Submitting an empty form reveals field messages. Roll 12A, a one-character name, an invalid email or an unselected course is rejected. If an institution uses alphanumeric roll numbers, change the stated policy rather than forcing inappropriate numeric conversion.

Unique roll-number checks, email ownership and actual record creation require a server and database. Client validation can be bypassed; repeat all rules and authorization server-side. The solution demonstrates complete field capture, validation state, guarded submission and safe feedback without falsely claiming a saved registration.

Conclusion: The student form validates the stated roll-number, name, email and course rules and displays a safe snapshot. A valid browser form alone does not establish uniqueness or save a registration.

Long 64
Question
Create an AngularJS registration form with Name, Age, Email and Password and validations. …
LongUnit 44.5 Angular forms & validation
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Build an AngularJS registration form with Name, Age, Email and Password. The illustrative rules are: a name of at least two characters, a whole-number age from 1 to 120, a required email-format value and a password of at least eight characters. The age range is an explicitly chosen demonstration policy because the question gives no range.

Aim and rules

Passwords are not displayed as plaintext, logged or stored in the result. A real application must perform registration on a server over HTTPS; this example only validates and displays nonsecret details.

Algorithm

Initialize data → attach named controls/validators → show errors on touch/submission → reject invalid/pending state and noninteger ages → copy name/age/email into a result → clear the password and reset interaction flags → show a safe confirmation.

Example: complete program

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="personRegistrationApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Validated registration</title></head>
<body ng-controller="RegistrationController as vm">
  <h1>Registration</h1>
  <form name="reg" ng-submit="vm.submit(reg)" novalidate>
    <label>Name <input name="fullName" ng-model="vm.data.name" required
      ng-minlength="2" autocomplete="name"></label>
    <p ng-show="(reg.fullName.$touched || reg.$submitted) && reg.fullName.$invalid">Enter a name of at least two characters.</p>
    <label>Age <input name="age" type="number" min="1" max="120" step="1"
      ng-model="vm.data.age" required></label>
    <p ng-show="(reg.age.$touched || reg.$submitted) && reg.age.$invalid">Enter a whole-number age from 1 to 120.</p>
    <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" ng-model="vm.data.email"
      required autocomplete="email"></label>
    <p ng-show="(reg.email.$touched || reg.$submitted) && reg.email.$invalid">Enter a valid email.</p>
    <label>Password <input name="password" type="password" ng-model="vm.data.password"
      required ng-minlength="8" ng-trim="false" autocomplete="new-password"></label>
    <p ng-show="(reg.password.$touched || reg.$submitted) && reg.password.$invalid">Password needs at least eight characters.</p>
    <button type="submit">Validate</button>
  </form>
  <p role="alert" ng-bind="vm.error"></p>
  <section ng-if="vm.result"><h2>Entered details</h2>
    <p>Name: {{vm.result.name}}</p><p>Age: {{vm.result.age}}</p>
    <p>Email: {{vm.result.email}}</p><p>Password: hidden for safety.</p>
    <p>Demo only; no account was created.</p>
  </section>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('personRegistrationApp', []).controller('RegistrationController', function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.data = {name: '', age: null, email: '', password: ''};
      vm.result = null; vm.error = '';
      vm.submit = function(form) {
        vm.result = null;
        var age = vm.data.age;
        if (form.$invalid || form.$pending || !Number.isInteger(age) || age < 1 || age > 120) {
          vm.error = 'Please correct all registration fields.'; return;
        }
        vm.error = '';
        vm.result = {name: vm.data.name, age: age, email: vm.data.email};
        vm.data.password = '';
        form.$setPristine(); form.$setUntouched();
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Working and sample output

AngularJS parses the number input into a numeric model. The explicit integer/range check also documents the business rule. novalidate lets AngularJS control feedback, while (field.$touched || form.$submitted) prevents errors from appearing on every untouched field immediately after page load.

Input: Asha Patel, 20, [email protected] and a password of at least eight characters. Output: Name Asha Patel; Age 20; Email [email protected]; Password hidden; demo notice. Age 0, 121 or 20.5 is rejected. Resetting pristine/untouched flags after clearing the password prevents an immediate “password required” message beside a successful demo result; it does not falsely make the now-empty field valid.

Limitations / precautions — security

ng-trim="false" preserves the intended password exactly. The minimum length is pedagogical and should be replaced by the application's security policy. Neither email syntax nor client validity proves identity. A backend must validate again, enforce uniqueness, hash passwords appropriately and create the account. The example separates safe result display from credential handling and makes all validation assumptions explicit.

Conclusion: Name, age and email can be displayed after validation, while the password remains hidden. Explicit limits and private credential handling separate the classroom demonstration from a real registration service.

Question
Create a sign-up form (username, password) using AngularJS with validation of empty fields. …
LongUnit 44.5 Angular forms & validation
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Create an AngularJS sign-up form with username and password, validating empty fields. Both controls are required. Username uses AngularJS's ordinary text trimming, so a whitespace-only username is treated as empty. The password is preserved exactly rather than silently trimmed; this exercise checks nonempty input, while a production system should apply its explicit password policy.

Aim and exact validation scope

The page displays only a safe demo confirmation. It does not create an account, prove username availability or authenticate the user.

Algorithm

Initialize two empty strings → bind required controls → track touched/submitted state → reject an invalid or pending form → capture only the username for feedback → clear the password → reset interaction flags. No raw credential is copied into the result.

Example: complete program

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="signupApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Sign-up validation</title></head>
<body ng-controller="SignupController as vm">
  <h1>Sign up</h1>
  <form name="signupForm" ng-submit="vm.submit(signupForm)" novalidate>
    <label>Username <input name="username" ng-model="vm.form.username"
      required autocomplete="username"></label>
    <p ng-show="(signupForm.username.$touched || signupForm.$submitted) && signupForm.username.$error.required">
      Username cannot be empty.
    </p>
    <label>Password <input name="password" type="password"
      ng-model="vm.form.password" required ng-trim="false" autocomplete="new-password"></label>
    <p ng-show="(signupForm.password.$touched || signupForm.$submitted) && signupForm.password.$error.required">
      Password cannot be empty.
    </p>
    <button type="submit">Validate sign-up</button>
  </form>
  <p role="alert" ng-bind="vm.error"></p>
  <p role="status" ng-if="vm.validatedName">
    Details validated for {{vm.validatedName}}. Demo only: no account created.
  </p>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('signupApp', []).controller('SignupController', function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.form = {username: '', password: ''};
      vm.validatedName = ''; vm.error = '';
      vm.submit = function(form) {
        vm.validatedName = '';
        if (form.$invalid || form.$pending || !vm.form.username || !vm.form.password) {
          vm.error = 'Both fields are required.'; return;
        }
        vm.error = '';
        vm.validatedName = vm.form.username;
        vm.form.password = '';
        form.$setPristine(); form.$setUntouched();
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Explanation and sample cases

The form's name exposes signupForm; its controls expose signupForm.username and signupForm.password. required adds each empty-value rule, and $error.required selects the corresponding message. A submit attempt marks the form submitted, so blank-field errors become visible even before a blur event.

Input Expected behavior
Both empty Both required messages; no confirmation
Username supplied, password empty Password error
Whitespace-only username Treated as empty by the text binding
asha01 and a nonempty password Username-only validation confirmation

After a successful check, the password input is cleared. $setPristine and $setUntouched reset feedback timing, not the underlying required validator; the cleared password remains invalid for a subsequent submission until re-entered.

Limitations / precautions — security

An all-space password is not an empty string under this minimal policy; a real application must decide whether to reject it without silently changing the user's secret. Add a considered password policy, server-side username uniqueness checks, rate limiting and secure password hashing when implementing actual registration. Never display the password with ng-bind, include it in a URL or store it in localStorage.

This answer directly meets the empty-field requirement using AngularJS control states and guarded submission, while clearly separating a classroom form from a real account-creation system.

Conclusion: Required controls and a guarded submission implement the requested empty-field checks. Actual sign-up additionally requires server-side policy, uniqueness checks and secure credential handling.

Question
Create an AngularJS login form with email and password and validation. …
LongUnit 44.5 Angular forms & validation
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Create an AngularJS login form with email and password. Require a valid email-format value and a nonempty password, and show well-timed errors. Since there is no backend in the question, this complete example validates input but explicitly reports not authenticated; it must not accept a hardcoded password and call that secure login.

Aim and validation boundary

Unlike sign-up, login should not arbitrarily impose a new minimum password length that could reject existing legitimate credentials. Preserve the password exactly and send it only to a trusted HTTPS endpoint in a real integration.

Algorithm

Initialize email/password → bind named controls → validate required/email rules → reject invalid or pending state → show a demo-only validation status → clear the password and reset interaction flags. For production, replace the demo branch with an asynchronous backend login request and explicit success/failure handling.

Example: complete program

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="loginApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>AngularJS login form</title></head>
<body ng-controller="LoginController as vm">
  <h1>Login</h1>
  <form name="loginForm" ng-submit="vm.login(loginForm)" novalidate>
    <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" required autocomplete="username"
      ng-model="vm.credentials.email"></label>
    <p ng-show="(loginForm.email.$touched || loginForm.$submitted) && loginForm.email.$error.required">Email is required.</p>
    <p ng-show="(loginForm.email.$touched || loginForm.$submitted) && loginForm.email.$error.email">Enter a valid email format.</p>
    <label>Password <input name="password" type="password" required ng-trim="false"
      autocomplete="current-password" ng-model="vm.credentials.password"></label>
    <p ng-show="(loginForm.password.$touched || loginForm.$submitted) && loginForm.password.$error.required">Password is required.</p>
    <button type="submit">Validate login input</button>
  </form>
  <p role="alert" ng-bind="vm.error"></p>
  <p role="status" ng-bind="vm.status"></p>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('loginApp', []).controller('LoginController', function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.credentials = {email: '', password: ''};
      vm.error = ''; vm.status = '';
      vm.login = function(form) {
        vm.status = '';
        if (form.$invalid || form.$pending || !vm.credentials.password) {
          vm.error = 'Enter a valid email and your password.'; return;
        }
        vm.error = '';
        vm.status = 'Input validated. Demo only: not authenticated.';
        vm.credentials.password = '';
        form.$setPristine(); form.$setUntouched();
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Working and expected behavior

type="email" activates AngularJS email validation and required rejects empty controls. The named form gives access to each failed rule. novalidate avoids competing native browser bubbles, leaving AngularJS to provide the messages. ng-submit covers keyboard and button submission without reloading a form that has no action URL.

Input: [email protected] plus a nonempty password. Output: Input validated. Demo only: not authenticated. The password is cleared and never printed. An empty email, not-an-email or an empty password prevents this status. Email syntax alone neither proves the account exists nor verifies ownership.

Limitations / precautions — real authentication and error handling

A production handler should call an HTTPS API, disable duplicate submissions while pending, handle network/server errors and restore UI state when the request finishes. The backend compares a stored secure password hash, enforces rate limits and creates a session. A generic invalid-credentials message is often preferable to revealing whether an email is registered.

Never put credentials in a GET query string, browser storage, logs or a displayed JSON object. A secure cookie-based session also requires appropriate cookie flags and CSRF considerations; client-visible state is not authorization.

Conclusion: The form correctly captures and validates the requested credentials with AngularJS while respecting the boundary between UI validation and authentication. The legacy framework's ended official support should also be considered before using it in a new real-world login system.
