Question
Write Angular JS code which accepts and validates Student Name, Email Address and Mobile No. from the user. …
LongUnit 44.5 Angular forms & validation
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Accept and validate Student Name, Email Address and Mobile No. using AngularJS. Name must be nonempty, email must pass the framework's email-format validator, and mobile is treated as text, not a number, because phone numbers are identifiers rather than quantities.

Aim and validation assumptions

Explicit regional assumption: this educational example accepts an Indian domestic mobile number of 10 digits beginning with 6–9, without spaces or a +91 prefix. The question does not specify an international format; a production application should normalize/validate according to its actual supported countries rather than use one global pattern.

Algorithm

Initialize fields → bind named controls → apply required/email/pattern rules → reveal field errors after touch or submit → reject invalid/pending state → create a safe snapshot of valid contact information → show a demo result.

Example: complete program

Save beside a local AngularJS 1.8.x angular.min.js.

HTML · study example
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" ng-app="contactApp">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Student contact validation</title></head>
<body ng-controller="ContactController as vm">
  <h1>Student contact details</h1>
  <form name="contactForm" ng-submit="vm.submit(contactForm)" novalidate>
    <label>Student Name <input name="studentName" ng-model="vm.student.name"
      required autocomplete="name"></label>
    <p ng-show="(contactForm.studentName.$touched || contactForm.$submitted) && contactForm.studentName.$invalid">Student name is required.</p>
    <label>Email Address <input name="email" type="email" ng-model="vm.student.email"
      required autocomplete="email"></label>
    <p ng-show="(contactForm.email.$touched || contactForm.$submitted) && contactForm.email.$invalid">Enter a valid email address.</p>
    <label>Mobile No. <input name="mobile" type="tel" inputmode="tel"
      ng-model="vm.student.mobile" required ng-pattern="/^[6-9][0-9]{9}$/"
      autocomplete="tel-national" aria-describedby="mobileHelp"></label>
    <p id="mobileHelp">Use 10 digits, starting with 6–9; omit +91.</p>
    <p ng-show="(contactForm.mobile.$touched || contactForm.$submitted) && contactForm.mobile.$invalid">Enter a valid 10-digit mobile number.</p>
    <button type="submit">Validate contact</button>
  </form>
  <p role="alert" ng-bind="vm.error"></p>
  <section ng-if="vm.result"><h2>Validated input</h2>
    <p>{{vm.result.name}}</p><p>{{vm.result.email}}</p><p>{{vm.result.mobile}}</p>
    <p>Demo only: ownership is not verified and nothing is saved.</p>
  </section>
  <script src="angular.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    angular.module('contactApp', []).controller('ContactController', function() {
      var vm = this;
      vm.student = {name: '', email: '', mobile: ''}; vm.result = null; vm.error = '';
      vm.submit = function(form) {
        vm.result = null;
        if (form.$invalid || form.$pending) {
          vm.error = 'Correct the contact fields before continuing.'; return;
        }
        vm.error = '';
        vm.result = angular.copy(vm.student);
      };
    });
  </script>
</body></html>

Pattern explanation and tests

^ anchors the start; [6-9] permits the first digit; [0-9]{9} requires nine further digits; $ anchors the end. Without anchors, a valid-looking substring inside a longer invalid value could be accepted. type="tel" provides an appropriate control but does not itself validate telephone formats.

Illustrative valid input: Asha Patel, [email protected], 9876543210. The result shows those three strings with a demo notice. A nine-digit value, alphabetic characters, an 11-digit value, or +91 under the stated local-only policy is rejected. A blank or whitespace-only name is invalid; no ASCII-only name pattern is imposed, so culturally varied names are not unnecessarily excluded.

Limitations / precautions — security, privacy

Format validity does not prove that the student owns the email address or phone number; ownership needs a verification workflow when required. Repeat validation on the server, avoid unnecessary logging and obtain appropriate consent for using contact data. A broader international application needs country-aware parsing, not a more permissive unanchored regex. This solution gives complete field binding, clear rules and feedback while making its phone-format assumption explicit.

Conclusion: The form validates the requested name, email and mobile fields under a stated local-number policy. Format checks do not prove ownership, so production use requires server validation and appropriate verification.

Long 68
Question
Differentiate between Template-driven Forms and Reactive Forms. …
LongUnit 44.5 Angular forms & validation
⛶
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter
Answer:

Introduction: Template-driven forms in modern Angular build the form model primarily through template directives such as ngModel and NgForm. Reactive forms define an explicit model in TypeScript using FormControl, FormGroup and FormArray, then connect it to the template. Both are modern Angular approaches; neither is AngularJS's $scope form system.

Ambiguity note: The two approaches are compared for modern Angular, not AngularJS 1.x. The worked program states the relevant FormsModule and ReactiveFormsModule imports.

Detailed comparison

Basis Template-driven Reactive
Main import FormsModule ReactiveFormsModule
Model declaration Largely created by template directives Explicit component/service objects
Control binding [(ngModel)], unique name inside a form [formControl], formControlName
Form binding #f="ngForm" [formGroup]="form"
Validation Attributes/directives and custom validators Validator functions and model configuration
State access Template references / NgForm FormGroup/FormControl APIs
Dynamic structures Possible, but can become cumbersome FormArray/dynamic composition are natural
Testing Often needs rendered template/directive setup Model and validators can be tested directly
Data streams Available through directive/control APIs valueChanges / statusChanges fit explicit workflows
Typical fit Small straightforward forms Large, dynamic or complex validation workflows

Reactive forms are not automatically more secure; both run in the client. Their explicit model updates are synchronous at the form-model API level, while template-driven model creation/registration involves the template lifecycle. Do not describe template-driven forms as inherently untestable or incapable of validation.

Example: complete side-by-side implementation

Use an Angular 17 CLI browser project with standard polyfills and <app-root> in index.html. Both forms request a name of at least two non-padding characters and display a local result.

Modern Angular · TypeScript
import {Component} from '@angular/core';
import {CommonModule} from '@angular/common';
import {FormsModule, NgForm, ReactiveFormsModule, FormControl,
  FormGroup, Validators} from '@angular/forms';
import {bootstrapApplication} from '@angular/platform-browser';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root', standalone: true,
  imports: [CommonModule, FormsModule, ReactiveFormsModule],
  template: `<h1>Two form approaches</h1>
    <form #tf="ngForm" (ngSubmit)="saveTemplate(tf)">
      <h2>Template-driven</h2>
      <label>Name <input name="studentName" [(ngModel)]="templateName"
        required minlength="2" #tn="ngModel"></label>
      <p *ngIf="(tn.touched || tf.submitted) && tn.invalid">Enter at least two characters.</p>
      <button type="submit">Save template form</button>
      <p role="status">{{templateMessage}}</p>
    </form>
    <form [formGroup]="reactiveForm" (ngSubmit)="saveReactive()">
      <h2>Reactive</h2>
      <label>Name <input formControlName="studentName"></label>
      <p *ngIf="reactiveForm.controls.studentName.touched && reactiveForm.controls.studentName.invalid">
        Enter at least two characters.
      </p>
      <button type="submit">Save reactive form</button>
      <p role="status">{{reactiveMessage}}</p>
    </form>`
})
class AppComponent {
  templateName = ''; templateMessage = ''; reactiveMessage = '';
  reactiveForm = new FormGroup({
    studentName: new FormControl('', {nonNullable: true,
      validators: [Validators.required, Validators.minLength(2)]})
  });
  saveTemplate(form: NgForm) {
    const name = this.templateName.trim();
    if (form.invalid || name.length < 2) {
      this.templateMessage = 'Enter at least two non-padding name characters.'; return;
    }
    this.templateMessage = `Validated: ${name}. Demo only.`;
  }
  saveReactive() {
    this.reactiveForm.markAllAsTouched();
    const name = this.reactiveForm.getRawValue().studentName.trim();
    if (this.reactiveForm.invalid || name.length < 2) {
      this.reactiveMessage = 'Enter at least two non-padding name characters.'; return;
    }
    this.reactiveMessage = `Validated: ${name}. Demo only.`;
  }
}
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(error => console.error(error));

Algorithm and observations

For the template-driven form, Angular registers the named ngModel control and derives its validity from attributes. For the reactive form, the TypeScript constructor configuration supplies validators, and formControlName connects the input to the existing control. Both submit handlers inspect state, reject whitespace-only/too-short names and display a non-persistence confirmation.

Entering Asha and submitting either form displays Validated: Asha. Demo only. Empty input or one character is invalid. Additional trimming checks are explicit because required and minLength alone are not complete semantic name validation. In a larger reactive form, move such rules into reusable custom validators; template-driven forms can wrap validators in directives.

Limitations / precautions — precautions

Do not combine ngModel and reactive-control binding on the same input. Use unique names in template-driven forms, correct control paths in reactive forms and cleanup for subscriptions you create manually. Form state and disabled buttons never replace backend validation or authorization. Select the simpler approach that meets complexity and testing needs, rather than assuming one form style is universally correct.

Conclusion: Template-driven forms emphasize declarative template setup; reactive forms emphasize explicit typed control models and programmatic composition. Choose according to form complexity, testing and state-management needs.
